***2025(9) CPT.** While the model the author presented produced Hessian matrices with small gradients, a concerning issue arose during the jittering analysis: jittering produced two clouds of model solutions at or near the MLE with OFLs that differed by 5,000 t. The author explained that the difference in OFLs resulted from differences in the terminal year estimates of MMB, driven by differences in recent recruitment estimates. In order to determine whether the absence of the 2020 survey data point is contributing to this issue, the CPT requested seeing the results of the jittering analysis from the accepted model but only including data through 2019.*

This analysis is presented as `Model 26.1c` (Section E), and the answer is that the absence of the 2020 survey point is not the source of the problem: truncating the data to 2019 leaves the model less stable, not more, with ten distinct minima against six and only 1.1 percent of converged runs recovering the best fit. The multimodality itself persists in the 2026 model, with six minima and a directed OFL spanning 81.8 to 90.6 kt across the jitter runs of the author-preferred model. See also the response to the May 2026 CPT report above.


***2025(9) CPT.** For future work in which results are shown from the same model configuration using different size-at-maturity, the CPT recommended against running separate jittering analyses for each scenario. Instead, after jittering is complete for the first scenario and the putative MLE has been identified, the parameter estimates from that run should be used for all comparisons that differ only in the size-at-maturity scenario because the MLE would be the same for all such scenarios (i.e., the size-at-maturity scenario should not affect the parameter estimates).*

No model presented this cycle differs from another only in the size-at-maturity scenario, so the situation the recommendation addresses does not arise. The three maturity definitions are compared within the Tier 4 model (Table \@ref(tab:tier4-currencies)), which is applied to the smoothed survey series and involves no re-estimation.


***2025(9) CPT.** The CPT further requested that the author investigate whether it is necessary to use the same number of size bins for males and females, noting that the BBRKC model uses different numbers of bins for the sexes.*

This was not undertaken for this cycle.


***2025(9) CPT.** There is a strong consensus by the CPT that the best available scientific information supports the conclusion that the status quo definition is not appropriate in terms of conserving the reproductive potential for the stock, or in terms of supporting optimal yield of commercial-sized animals for harvest. The CPT therefore again recommended a change to the definition of maturity for this stock, from morphometric maturity to >= 95 mm CW.*

The CPT and SSC have not agreed on this question. The CPT recommended the >= 95 mm definition in 2024 and again in September 2025. On both occasions the SSC concluded that the available region-specific information was not sufficient to support the change, and directed that morphometric maturity remain the basis. The October 2025 SSC report is the most recent direction and is what the recommendation follows.

The authors follow the SSC's direction: morphometrically mature male biomass is the recommended definition for the Tier 4 model and the harvest specification. The CPT's concern remains valid. A large fraction of the population is morphometrically mature at sizes the fishery does not retain, so reference points on this definition can permit removing essentially all large males while the trend in large males is negative. The large-male and preferred-male definitions are therefore reported alongside the recommendation. For scale, the recommended OFL of `r .f(ofl_2026, 2)` kt is `r .f(100*ofl_2026/survey_large_2026, 0)` percent of observed large-male (>= 95 mm) survey biomass and `r .f(100*ofl_2026/survey_pref_2026, 0)` percent of preferred-male (> 101 mm) biomass in 2026 (Table \@ref(tab:survey-currencies)). This bears on the ABC buffer in Section G.


***2025(6) SSC.** The maximin analysis should be completed assuming a Ricker stock-recruitment relationship, but including the same compensation ratios as the original Clark (1991) analysis.* 

The Ricker curves used in Clark were implemented in the maximin analysis presented last cycle (and now published in Fisheries Research: Szuwalski and Punt (2025) “Spawning-biomass-per-recruit proxies for fisheries reference points under multiple axes of uncertainty”). Incorporating these into the analysis shifted the SPR% from ~36% to ~34%.


***2025(6) SSC.** As the figures presented on the updated 1991+ catch data appear to indicate substantial differences in male discards, the SSC requests that the September document more clearly describe changes in the discard estimation and accounting process.*

A presentation from January 2025 from ADF&G (available on the council website) noted that the largest changes occurred for total catch through implementing consistent data filtering, expansion using directed pot lifts, and adjustments to biological strata. This process now allows for the production of a data file with all years of available data for each assessment cycle, instead of single years appended to an existing data file. An apparent shift upwards in discards of males from the directed fishery results primarily from a change in when discard mortality is applied (before input into the data file [before 2025] or within the assessment code itself [after 2025]).


***2025(6) SSC.** Given the findings described in Mullowney and Baker (2021) from Canadian research indicating that the molt to maturity may occur at smaller sizes when lower densities of large males are present, it would be useful to determine if there is evidence for the same process occurring in EBS snow crab, and whether fishing mortality on the large males is consistently high enough to result in a strong effect. Further, it would be useful to evaluate whether clutch fullness may be related to size at maturity or the abundance of large-sized crab.*

*Given that natural mortality events seem to switch among years and sexes depending on the model or input data, it would be prudent to investigate whether it is possible to estimate a direct link between natural mortality and a bottom temperature covariate of appropriate spatial and temporal scale.*

A manuscript describing both of these relationships for Bering Sea snow crab was presented in May/June 2024 (Figure 3; “Density dependence can modulate climate change impacts on populations”) and was published in 2026 (Szuwalski et al., 2026). In that manuscript, warmer temperatures were associated with elevated mortality and higher densities of large males were associated with lower probabilities of terminally molting at
size. 

The SSC responded to this presentation with the following text: “The SSC emphasizes that projections of climate change impacts, while useful, are highly uncertain and. . . caution should be used when presenting
these results.”

Clutch fullness does not appear to be related to the abundance of large-size crab based on analyses in “Spatial depletion rates in the eastern Bering Sea snow crab fishery” (also presented in May 2024 and now in review for external publication). It is unclear if there is any relationship between clutch fullness and recruitment, though preliminary analyses suggest clutch fullness is not an important covariate for predicting recruitment strength.

These analyses were conducted under the legacy maturity workflow. The Kodiak laboratory has since revised that workflow, and the revision is used in every model presented here, so the analyses should be revisited using the new series.


***2025(6) SSC.** To explore development of an ABC control rule, the SSC requests that a yield per recruit analysis be developed for snow crab.*

Not completed. The SSC restated this request with a detailed specification in October 2025 and again in June 2026. See the response to the October 2025 comment above.


***2024(10) SSC.** SSC recommends standardizing the approach to the Tier 4 fallback across BBRKC, Tanner and snow crab assessments so that the same methods are used for each including all mature male biomass, a BMSY proxy based on the time-series of REMA-smoothed survey estimates and an FMSY proxy based on the best estimate of natural mortality (from the Tier 3 model). As the SSC intends the Tier 4 calculation only as a fallback if the Tier 3 analysis fails to converge, no other Tier 4 calculations need to be included in future assessments.*

In the 2025 document, Tier 4 harvest control rules were applied to REMA-smoothed survey biomass estimates of three different size ranges: morphometrically mature males, large males (>= 95 mm), and preferred males (> 101 mm). The target biomass was set as the average of the time series from 1982 to 2024 and the target fishing mortality was set as 0.27, the median of the prior on natural mortality used in the integrated assessment. No kink exists in this harvest control rule. The resulting OFLs were 28.41 kt, 8.64 kt, and 6.11 kt for morphometric, large, and preferred males, respectively.

The same three maturity definitions are retained, and the Tier 4 model is described in Section F. Following the October 2025 SSC recommendation, morphometrically mature male biomass is the basis of the recommended specification, with the other two definitions shown for comparison. The author-recommended approach departs from the standard in one respect: it applies the Baranov catch equation instead of incorrectly multiplying F times biomass. The standard linear result is reported alongside it in Table \@ref(tab:tier4-currencies) to preserve the comparison across BSAI crab stocks, and the ramped-rule and linear-equation alternatives are also reported so the effect of each change can be compared.


***2024(10) SSC.** The SSC highlighted that more research is needed on the basic reproductive biology of snow crab, specifically addressing the question of whether small males can and do mate with large females and produce progeny that will be large males under the right environmental conditions. The SSC strongly supports the proposed collaborative research to explore in situ observations of mating crab using a camera sled.*

We agree. Camera-sled observations (Weems et al., in preparation) recorded small morphometrically mature males grasping mature females in the eastern Bering Sea (n = 21). Broader sampling coverage is needed before conclusions can be drawn.


***2024(10) SSC.** The highest priority would be to continue to refine the Maximin analysis as requested by the SSC in June 2024, specifically using values of steepness of 0.50, 0.67, and 0.80, and considering both the Beverton-Holt and Ricker stock recruitment relationships. The yield analysis also indicated that fishing mortality rates much lower than F35% achieved a high percentage of MSY, indicating potential flexibility in specifying reference points. The SSC suggested that some type of collaborative work during the spring, perhaps including SSC members and/or others might facilitate additional progress on this topic. The SSC is interested in developing a wider range of options for reference points for snow crab for consideration in the next assessment cycle.*

The analysis was not extended beyond what was presented in appendix A of the 2024 SAFE and would be of limited use until we know more about reproductive contribution of large male snow crab. The specific values for steepness recommended by the SSC do not match estimates or available data on the reproductive dynamics of snow crab. We suggest focusing efforts on understanding the dynamics of large males given the reliance of the fishery on large males that are at historical lows.


***2024(10) SSC.** The SSC again requests an analysis of the probability of maturing/terminal molt which addresses the observation error in these data and the lack of a monotonically increasing curve. A hierarchical analysis that treats years as random effects might be a starting point. The SSC would also like to better understand the sampling design for the molt data and is concerned about the weighting of the spatial samples in the analysis. Weighting should be based on abundance if the sampling rate differs by area (which it would, unless abundance were uniform and/or the targets were in direct proportion to abundance).*

The Kodiak lab presented its workflow to the CPT in January 2025, with a summary to the SSC. The revised workflow fits a spatiotemporal `sdmTMB` model to the chela-based maturity classifications, borrowing information across years and locations for size bins with sparse data, and incorporates spatial weighting directly. The CPT recommended it in May 2026 and it is used in every model except the rolled-forward 2025 model, which retains the legacy series, so the two can be compared directly (Figure \@ref(fig:predmat)). The revised series shows a markedly weaker temporal trend at intermediate sizes. Observation error is still not propagated: the ogive enters as a fixed input, not as data with a likelihood. See Ryznar (in prep).


***2024(10) SSC.** Investigate whether there is information outside the assessment model (e.g., larval or post-settlement data) or in the model, supporting estimated skewed sex-ratios at recruitment and the mismatch between recent large recruitments for males and females occurring in different years. Explore whether the estimated large differences in male and female recruitment years could be related to the lack of fit to molt-increment data.*

No new information has come to light on why this might be the case. Previous discussion centered on the possibility that different spatial distributions by sex of small crab expose them to different environments, altering perceived recruitment five years after settlement. That is an interesting scientific question, but solving it will not address the central management problem: commercially preferred males are at historic lows. Removing the females focuses the model on that problem, and `Model 26.2` does so as a sensitivity (Section E). The related request, to examine whether the male-female divergence connects to the lack of fit to the molt-increment data, has not been taken up; removing the females sets it aside instead of answering it.


***2024(10) SSC.** Geostatistical (e.g. VAST) modeling of trawl survey data including both the NBS and EBS should be prioritized. This could help understand some of the inconsistent recruitment/growth trends observed in recent years as well as prepare for potential changes in stock distribution or productivity under future warming of the Bering Sea. Geostatistical modeling should evaluate alternative error distributions and other model configurations as appropriate.*

The Kodiak lab presented indices for mature females and large males using geostatistical modeling at the May 2025 CPT. The northern Bering Sea is not included in the geostatistical modeling because estimates would have to be extrapolated in years when that area was not surveyed.



***2024(6) CPT.** Tier 4 fallback - CPT supports: The author suggested an alternative for snow crab to the basic Tier 4 calculation that is being brought forward for other stocks. Specifically, a fallback Tier 4 option would be calculated as the vulnerable biomass in this year’s survey (not smoothed, and vulnerable defined by a cutoff of 95 mm CW), decremented by the proportion of natural mortality that occurs between the time of the survey and the fishery, and M applied as the proxy for FMSY to calculate the Tier 4 OFL. The motivations identified for using the annual survey design-based estimate of vulnerable biomass rather than a REMA smooth through the survey time series were: 1) that the high number of positive stations for snow crab on survey (238 stations in 2023) make the design-based estimate a robust measure of annual biomass; and 2) that the large interannual fluctuations in biomass observed in some recent years would be poorly captured by a smooth. The motivation for decrementing the biomass estimate by the proportion of natural mortality occurring between the survey and the fishery is that failing to account for this mortality could lead to unintentionally high values of F if the Tier 4 fallback was used.*

The Tier 4 model is presented in Section F and is the basis of the recommended harvest specification for 2026/27. It follows the standardized approach the SSC set out in October 2024 rather than the decremented, unsmoothed variant described in this comment: it uses all morphometrically mature male biomass, a B~MSY~ proxy from the REMA-smoothed survey series, and the best estimate of natural mortality as the F~MSY~ proxy, and it is not decremented for mortality between the survey and the fishery.


***2024(6) SSC.** Concerning the GMACS assessment model, the SSC continues to recommend that the assessment author explore ways to incorporate the molt to maturity data in the model in a way that reflects the observation error associated with those estimates. An analysis in a GLMM modeling framework, which treats years as random effects, would provide smoother estimates, accommodate differing sample sizes by year and length, and deal appropriately with years in which data are missing. Another possibility that was suggested in the CPT report was to include the annual observed probabilities of terminal molt as data and then fit them, as in the Tanner crab assessment.*

Observation error is still not propagated into the assessment: the maturity ogive enters the model as a fixed input rather than as data with an associated likelihood. The Kodiak laboratory presented its workflow to the Plan Team in May 2026. That workflow was recommended for adoption and is used in every model presented here (see the response to the October 2025 comment above). The Tanner crab assessment fits to the maturity data with its observation error, and doing the same for snow crab remains an area for improvement. Given the complexity of the GMACS model, this is not a priority until convergence problems are resolved.


***2024(6) SSC.** The SSC recommends that this model be brought forward in the fall but requests that an additional Tier 4 model be provided for comparison, as recommended in the Simpler Modeling Workshop report and requested in the SSC’s June 2023 and October 2023 Reports. This additional model would use the random effects model (REMA) to smooth survey estimates and would not decrement with natural mortality.*

A Tier 4 assessment using the REMA model to smooth the survey estimates, without a decrement for natural mortality, has been included in each assessment since 2024. It is presented in Section F, where it is the basis of the recommended specification rather than a comparison.

\newpage

# C. Introduction

Studies and data relevant to key population and fishery processes are discussed below to provide background for the modeling choices made in this assessment. A description of the model is available in the GMACS repository (https://github.com/GMACS-project), and the files needed to reproduce this assessment are archived in a separate repository. Both are linked in Section J.

## Distribution
Snow crab (*Chionoecetes opilio*) are distributed on the continental shelf of the Bering Sea, Chukchi Sea, and in the western Atlantic Ocean as far south as Maine.  In the Bering Sea, snow crab are distributed widely over the shelf and are common at depths less than ~200 meters (see tech memo; Zacher et al., 2026). Smaller crab tend to occupy more inshore northern regions and mature crab occupy deeper areas to the south of the juveniles (see Zacher et al., 2026; Zheng et al. 2001). The eastern Bering Sea population within U.S. waters is managed as a single stock. However, the distribution of the population may extend into Russian waters to an unknown degree.

## Natural Mortality

Relatively few targeted studies exist to determine natural mortality for snow crab in the Bering Sea.  Nevissi, et al. (1995) used radiometric techniques to estimate shell age from last molt (Figure \@ref(fig:nevissi)).  The total sample size was 21 male crab (a combination of Tanner and snow crab) from a collection of 105 male crab from various hauls in the 1992 National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) Bering Sea survey. Representative samples for the 5 shell condition categories were collected from the available crab.  Shell condition 5 crab (SC5 = very, very old shell) had a maximum age of 6.85 years (s.d. 0.58, 95% CI approximately 5.69 to 8.01 years; carapace width of 110 mm).  The average age of 6 crab with SC4 (very old shell) and SC5, was 4.95 years (range: 2.70 to 6.85 years).  Given the small sample size, this maximum age may not represent the 1.5th percentile of the population that is approximately equivalent to Hoenig's method (1983). Tag recovery evidence from eastern Canada revealed observed maximum ages in exploited populations of 17-19 years (Nevissi, et al. 1995, Sainte-Marie 2002).  A maximum time at large of 11 years for tag returns of terminally molted mature male snow crab in the North Atlantic has been recorded since tagging started about 1993 (Fonseca, et al. 2008).  Fonseca, et al. (2008) estimated a maximum age of 7.8 years post terminal molt using data on dactyl wear.

```{r nevissi, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Radiometric estimates of shell age in male snow and Tanner crab collected during the NMFS survey of 1992. Reproduced from Ernst et al. (2005)'s presentation of Nevissi et al. (1995)."}
knitr::include_graphics("continuity/background/nevissi1.png")
```

In recent years, the mean for the prior for natural mortality used in the eastern Bering Sea snow crab assessment was based on the assumption that longevity would be at least 20 years in an unfished population of snow crab, informed by the studies above.  Under negative exponential depletion, the 99th percentile corresponding to age 20 of an unexploited population corresponds to a natural mortality rate of 0.23.  Using Hoenig's (1983) method a natural mortality equal to 0.23 corresponds to a maximum age of 18 years.

In contrast to the implied natural mortalities from the methodology used above, Murphy et al. (2018) estimated time-varying natural mortality for eastern Bering Sea snow crab with a mean of 0.49 for females and 0.36 for males based on the output of state-space models fit to NMFS survey data. Further, natural mortality estimates produced from empirical analyses by Then et al. (2015) and Hamel (2015) using similar assumed maximum ages as the methodology above produced natural mortalities larger than 0.23 (Table \@ref(tab:natm-empir)). Then et al. (2015) compared several major empirical estimation methods for M (including Hoenig's method) with an updated data set and found that maximum age was the best available predictor. A maximum age of 20 years corresponded to an M of ~0.315 in Then et al.'s analysis. Hamel (2015) developed priors in a similar manner to Then et al., but forced the regression of observed natural mortality onto maximum age through the intercept, which resulted in an M of ~0.27 for an assumed maximum age of 20 years.

```{r natm-empir, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Empirical M estimates, methods as rows and assumed maximum ages as columns.
# Was a pander table with a \label{} caption, which cross-references only in
# LaTeX output; rebuilt as flextable + run_autonum so Table \@ref(tab:natm-empir)
# resolves in Word as well (2026-08-31). Values unchanged.
natm_emp <- data.frame(
  Method = c("Then", "Hoenig (1983)", "Hoenig (2013)", "Hamel"),
  `23`   = c(0.277, 0.190, 0.194, 0.235),
  `20`   = c(0.315, 0.212, 0.223, 0.271),
  `17`   = c(0.365, 0.257, 0.261, 0.318),
  check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

flextable::flextable(natm_emp) |>
  # Straddles a page break, so flextable repeats the caption and its \label in
  # the longtable continuation head and the label is reported as multiply
  # defined. Keep caption and label on the first page only (2026-08-31).
  flextable::set_table_properties(opts_pdf = list(caption_repeat = FALSE)) |>
  flextable::colformat_double(j = c("23", "20", "17"), digits = 3) |>
  flextable::autofit() |>
  flextable::set_caption(
    caption = paste("Empirical estimates of natural mortality (per year) for a range",
                    "of methods over a range of assumed maximum ages (column headers).",
                    "These are empirical estimators, not output of any assessment",
                    "model."),
    autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "natm-empir"))
```

In addition to the results of empirical estimates of M from updated methodologies and state-space modeling by Murphy et al. (2018), inspection of the survey data suggests that natural mortality for mature individuals is higher than assumed. A fraction of the mature population (which are assumed not to grow, given evidence for a terminal molt) are not selected in the fishery (e.g. sizes 50-80 mm; Figure \@ref(fig:natm-mature)). Consequently, all mortality observed is 'natural'. The collapse in recruitment in the 1990s can be used as an instrument to understand natural mortality for mature individuals. The last large recruitment enters these size classes in the mid- to late-1990s and numbers of crab in these size classes return to low levels in less than 5 years.

```{r natm-mature, echo=FALSE, out.width="90%", fig.cap="Observed numbers at length of old-shell mature males by size class. The size bins presented are not vulnerable to the fishery, so all mortality observed in them is natural."}
knitr::include_graphics("continuity/background/old_shell_males_at_len.png")
```

The median value of the priors used in this assessment is set equal to values resulting from assuming a maximum age of 20 years and applying Hamel's methodology (0.271). A standard error of 0.0054 was used for initial priors and was estimated using the 95% CI of +-1.7 years on maximum age estimates from dactyl wear and tag return analysis in Fonseca, et al. (2008). Mortality events in 2018 and 2019 are estimated as additional mortality parameters applied by sex and maturity state to allow the model to fit recent population trends.

## Maturity

Maturity of females collected during the NMFS summer survey was determined by the shape of the abdomen, by the presence of brooded eggs, or egg remnants. Maturity for males was determined by chela height measurements, which were available most years starting from the 1989 survey (Otto 1998; Figure \@ref(fig:maturity-facet) & Figure \@ref(fig:maturity-facet-all)). Unless stated otherwise, mature male biomass means the biomass of morphometrically mature (large-clawed) males; the >= 95 mm and > 101 mm definitions are reported alongside it in Section F. A maturity curve for males was estimated using the average fraction mature based on chela height data and applied to years of survey data to estimate mature survey numbers that do not have chela height data available (see Richar and Foy, 2022 for details).

```{r maturity-facet, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Observed probability of having undergone terminal molt at size for new-shell male crab, based on chela height. Blue lines are earlier in the time series; red lines are the most recent."}
knitr::include_graphics("plots/maturity_facet.png")
```

```{r maturity-facet-all, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Observed probability of having undergone terminal molt at size for new-shell male crab, based on chela height. The red line is the median over all years; blue lines are individual years."}
knitr::include_graphics("plots/maturity_facet_all.png")
```

Bering Sea male snow crab appear to have a terminal molt to maturity based on hormone level data and findings from molt stage analysis via setagenesis (Tamone et al. 2005).  The models presented here assume a terminal molt for both males and females, which is supported by research on populations in the Bering Sea and the Atlantic Ocean (e.g. Dawe et al. 1991).

Mature male snow crab that do not molt may be important in reproduction.  Paul et al. (1995) found that old shell mature male Tanner crab out-competed new shell crab of the same size in breeding in a laboratory study.  Recently molted males did not breed even with no competition and may not breed until after ~100 days from molting (Paul et al. 1995).  Sainte-Marie et al. (2002) stated that only old shell males take part in mating for North Atlantic snow crab.

## Maturity and reproductive success

Bering Sea snow crab have historically been managed using morphometrically mature male biomass (MMB) as a proxy for reproductive potential. MMB is used for management because the fishery only retains large male crab, which are nearly 100% mature. Male snow crab are sperm conservers, using less than 4% of their sperm at each mating and females can mate with more than one male. The amount of stored sperm and clutch fullness varies with sex ratio (Sainte-Marie 2002).  If mating with only one male is inadequate to fertilize a full clutch, then females would need to mate with more than one male, necessitating a sex ratio closer to 1:1 in the mature population than if one male is assumed to be able to adequately fertilize multiple females. Although mature male biomass is currently the basis of management, some aspect of female reproduction is likely also an important indicator of reproductive potential of the stock.

 Clutch fullness is recorded for the females measured in the survey (see ESP; Fedewa et al., 2025). However, quantifying the reproductive potential of the female population from survey data can be difficult. For example, full clutches of unfertilized eggs may be extruded and appear normal to visual examination, and may be retained for several weeks or months by snow crab. Resorption of eggs may occur if not all eggs are extruded resulting in less than a full clutch.  Female snow crab at the time of the survey may have a full clutch of eggs that are unfertilized, resulting in overestimation of reproductive potential. Barren females may be a more obvious indication of low reproductive potential and increased in the early 1990s, decreased in the mid-1990s, then increased again in the late 1990s. The highest levels of barren females coincided with periods of high fishing mortality, but even then the proportion of barren females was low (see ESP; Fedewa et al., 2025). Biennial spawning is another confounding factor in determining the reproductive potential of snow crab. Laboratory analyses showed that female snow crab collected in waters colder than 1.5 degrees C from the Bering Sea spawn only every two years.

Further complicating the process of quantifying reproductive capacity, clutch fullness and fraction of unmated females may not account for the fraction of females that may have unfertilized eggs, since these cannot be detected by eye at the time of the survey.  The fraction of barren females observed in the survey may not be an accurate measure of fertilization success because females may retain unfertilized eggs for months after extrusion.  To examine this hypothesis, NMFS personnel sampled mature females from the Bering Sea in winter and held them in tanks until their eggs hatched in March of the same year (Rugolo et al. 2005).  All females then extruded a new clutch of eggs in the absence of males.  All eggs were retained until the crab were euthanized near the end of August.  Approximately 20% of the females had full clutches of unfertilized eggs.  The unfertilized eggs could not be distinguished from fertilized eggs by visual inspection at the time they were euthanized.  Indices of fertilized females based on the visual inspection method of assessing clutch fullness and percent unmated females may overestimate fertilized females.

## Growth

Several studies are available to estimate the growth per molt of male and female snow crab in the Bering Sea. These studies include:

1.  Transit study (2003); 14 crab
2.	Cooperative seasonality study; 6 crab
3.	Dutch Harbor holding study; 9 crab
4.	NMFS Kodiak holding study held less than 30 days;  6 crab
5.  NMFS Kodiak holding study 2016; 5 crab
6.  NMFS Kodiak holding study 2017; 70 crab.
7.  BSFRF/NMFS holding study 2018; 4 crab.
8.  BSFRF/NMFS holding study 2021; 177 crab.

In the "Transit study", pre- and post-molt measurements of 14 male crab that molted soon after being captured were collected.  The crab were measured when shells were still soft because all died after molting, so measurements may be underestimates of post-molt width (L. Rugolo, pers. com.). The holding studies include only data for crab held less than 30 days because growth of crab held until the next spring's molting was much lower. Crab missing more than two limbs were excluded due to other studies showing lower growth. Crab from the seasonal study were excluded that were measured less than 3 days after molting due to difficulty in measuring soft crab accurately (L. Rugolo, pers. comm.). In general, growth of snow crab in the Bering Sea appears to be greater than growth of some North Atlantic snow crab stocks (Sainte-Marie 1995).  Crab in their first few years of life may molt more than once per year, however, the smallest crab included in the Tier 3 model are approximately 4 years old and would be expected to molt annually.

## Management history

The subsections below summarize the State of Alaska harvest strategy, the history of the B~MSY~ reference point, and the history of the fishery.

## ADF&G harvest strategy

Before 2000, the Guideline Harvest Level (GHL) for retained crab only was a 58% harvest rate of the number of male crab over 101 mm CW estimated from the survey.  The minimum legal size limit for snow crab is 78 mm, however, the snow crab market generally only accepts crab greater than 101 mm.  In 2000, due to the decline in abundance and the declaration of the stock as overfished, the harvest rate for calculation of the GHL was reduced to 20% of male crab over 101 mm.  After 2000, a rebuilding strategy was developed based on simulations by Zheng et al. (2002) using survey biomass estimates. The realized retained catch often exceeded the GHL historically.

The Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) harvest strategy since 2000 sets harvest rate based on estimated mature biomass. The harvest rate scales with the status of the population relative to a proxy for B~*MSY*~, which is calculated as the average total mature biomass at the time of the survey from 1983 to present and MSST is one half the B~*MSY*~ proxy.  The harvest rate begins at 0.10 when total mature biomass exceeds 50% MSST (230 million lbs) and increases linearly to 0.225 when biomass is equal to or greater than the B~*MSY*~ proxy (Zheng et al. 2002).

\begin{equation}
 u =
 \begin{cases}
 Bycatch  & if \frac{TMB}{TMB_{MSY}} \leq 0.25 \\[3ex]
 \frac {0.225 ( \frac {TMB}{TMB_{MSY}} - \alpha)}{1-\alpha}  & if 0.25 < \frac {TMB}{TMB_{MSY}} < 1 \\[3ex]
 0.225 & if TMB >TMB_{MSY}
\end{cases}
\end{equation}

Where *TMB* is the total mature biomass and TMB~*BMSY*~ is the *TMB* associated with maximum sustainable yield. The maximum retained catch is set as the product of the exploitation rate, *u*, calculated from the above control rule and survey mature male biomass.  If the retained catch in numbers is greater than 58% of the estimated number of new shell crab greater than 101 mm plus 25% of the old shell crab greater than 101 mm, the catch is capped at 58%.

## History of BMSY

Prior to adoption of Amendment 24, B~*MSY*~ was defined as the average total mature biomass (males and females) estimated from the survey for the years 1983 to 1997 (921.6 million lbs; NPFMC 1998) and MSST was defined as 50% of B~*MSY*~. Currently, the biological reference point for biomass is calculated using a spawning biomass per recruit proxy, B~*35%*~ (Clark, 1993). B~*35%*~ is the biomass at which spawning biomass per recruit is 35% of unfished levels and has been shown to provide close to maximum sustainable yield for a range of stock productivities (Clark, 1993). Consequently, it is a commonly used target when a stock recruit relationship is unknown or unreliable.  The range of years of recruitment used to calculate biomass reference points is from 1982 to the present assessment year, minus 1. However, recent analyses suggest SPR-based reference points do not provide a meaningful constraint on the snow crab fishery when the probability of having undergone terminal molt is specified to reflect observations in the survey. This is because a large fraction of the population matures (and ceases growing) at a size smaller than is harvested by the fishery.

## Fishery history

Snow crab were harvested in the Bering Sea by the Japanese from the 1960s until 1980 when the Magnuson Act prohibited foreign fishing. After the closure to foreign fleets, retained catches increased from relatively low levels in the early 1980s (e.g.  `r round(as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==1982)$obs[1]),2)` kt during 1982) to historical highs in the 1990s (retained catches during 1991, 1992, and 1998 were `r round(as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==1991)$obs[1]),2)`, `r round(as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==1992)$obs[1]),2)`, and `r round(as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==1998)$obs[1]),2)` kt, respectively).  The stock was declared overfished in 1999 at which time retained catches dropped to levels similar to the early 1980s (e.g. `r round(as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==2000)$obs[1]),2)` kt). Retained catches slowly increased after 1999 before dropping again in 2016. Total allowable catches were reduced with the collapse of the population in 2021, the fishery was closed for the first time in 2022, and the closure continued through 2023. A small fishery occurred in 2024, with 2.15 kt retained, and a larger one in 2025, when the State set a total allowable catch of 4.22 kt and 4.13 kt was retained. <!-- TODO 2026: extend to the 2025/26 fishery once characterized (ADF&G retained ~4.1 kt in crab_year 2025). -->

Discard mortality from the directed fishery is the next largest source of mortality after retained catch and approximately tracks the retained catch. The highest estimated discard mortality occurred during 1990 at `r round(as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==1990)$obs[2]),2)` kt which was `r round(100*as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==1990)$obs[2])/ as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==1990)$obs[1]),2)`% of the retained catch during that year. Discard mortality in 2024 was `r round(as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==2024)$obs[2]),2)` kt. The directed fishery was closed in 2022 and 2023, so no directed discards were recorded in those years. Non-directed mortality continues to be very small at `r round(as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==2024)$obs[4]),2)` kt in 2024.

Discards from the directed pot fishery have been estimated from observer data since 1992 and have ranged from 11-100% of the magnitude of retained catch by numbers. Discards reached 50-100% of the magnitude of retained catch in the lead up to the collapse after the 2018-2019 heatwave because of the large year class entering the population. Female discarded catch has been very low compared to male discards and has not been a significant source of mortality. Discard mortality for the directed fishery is assumed to be 30%. Discard of snow crab in groundfish fisheries has been highest in the yellowfin sole trawl fishery, and decreases down through the flathead sole trawl fishery, Pacific cod bottom trawl fishery, rock sole trawl fishery, and the Pacific cod hook-and-line and pot fisheries, respectively (Figure \@ref(fig:bycatch)).  Bycatch in fisheries other than the groundfish trawl fishery has historically been relatively low. Discard mortality in the non-directed fisheries is taken as total in the models presented here: the trawl bycatch series enters the assessment with a discard mortality of 1, not the 0.8 applied when those removals are prepared. This treatment is intended. A cleaner approach for future cycles is to input the raw removals and apply discard mortality within GMACS, which would simplify sensitivity analyses to those rates. Size frequency data and catch per pot have been collected by observers on snow crab fishery vessels since 1992.  Observer coverage has been 10% on catcher vessels larger than 125 ft (since 2001), and 100% coverage on catcher processors (since 1992).

```{r bycatch, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Time series of non-directed bycatch from the groundfish fisheries by gear, in numbers of crab."}
knitr::include_graphics("plots/bycatch.png")
```

Several modifications to pot gear have been introduced to reduce bycatch mortality.  In the 1978/79 season, escape panels were required on pots used in the snow crab fishery to prevent ghost fishing.  Escape panels consist of an opening with one-half the perimeter of the tunnel eye laced with untreated cotton twine.  The size of the cotton laced panel was increased in 1991 to at least 18 inches in length.  No escape mechanisms for undersized crab were required until the 1997 season when at least one-third of one vertical surface of pots had to contain not less than 5 inches stretched mesh webbing or have no less than four circular rings of no less than 3 3/4 inches inside diameter.  In the 2001 season the escapement provisions for undersized crab were increased to at least eight escape rings of no less than 4 inches placed within one mesh measurement from the bottom of the pot, with four escape rings on each side of the two sides of a four-sided pot, or one-half of one side of the pot must have a side panel composed of not less than 5 1/4 inch stretched mesh webbing.

# D. Data

Updated time series of survey indices and size compositions were downloaded using the crabpack R package (Zacher et al., 2026). Retained, total, and discarded catch and relevant size composition data were updated from 1990 to present based on files provided by the State of Alaska. Non-directed bycatch data were updated from the NORPAC database.

## Catch data

Catch data and size composition of retained crab from the directed snow crab pot fishery for crab years 1982 to 2025 were used in this analysis (Table \@ref(tab:obscatch)). Time series of discarded catch from the directed fishery are fit, but size composition data are for total catch. The discard male catch was estimated for crab years 1982 to 1991 in the model using the estimated fishery selectivities based on the observer data for crab years 1992 to 2025. The discards prior to 1992 may be underestimated due to the lack of escape mechanisms for undersized crab in the pots before 1997. See Table \@ref(tab:datayears) for a summary of the catch data range.

## Survey biomass and size composition data
Estimates of the numbers of crab by sex and size from the annual eastern Bering Sea (EBS) bottom trawl survey conducted by NMFS (e.g. Figure \@ref(fig:n-at-len) & Figure \@ref(fig:n-at-len-f); see Lang et al., 2018 for materials and methods; see the most recent tech memo for detailed description) are used to calculate the primary indices of abundance used in this assessment. Additional survey stations were added in 1989, which could alter the interpretation of the catchability coefficient for the survey. Consequently, survey selectivity has been historically modeled in two 'eras' in the assessment (1982-1988, 1989-present). All survey data in this assessment used measured net widths instead of the fixed 50 ft net width based on Chilton et al.'s (2009) survey estimates. Carapace width and shell conditions were measured and reported for snow crab caught in the survey.

```{r n-at-len, echo=FALSE, out.width="86%", fig.cap="Raw total numbers at size of male crab observed in the survey. Blue are all numbers at size. Green are males > 101 mm carapace width, the industry-preferred size."}
knitr::include_graphics("plots/size_bins_comp_Kodiak_m.png")
```

```{r n-at-len-f, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Raw total numbers at size of immature and mature female crab observed in the survey, binned at 5 mm intervals."}
knitr::include_graphics("plots/n_at_l_f.png")
```

Mature male size composition data were calculated by multiplying the total numbers at length for new shell male crab by a vector of observed proportion of mature males at length. All old shell crab of both sexes were assumed to be mature.  New shell crab were demarcated as any crab with shell condition index <= 2. The biomass of new and old shell mature individuals was calculated by multiplying the vector of numbers at length by weight at length. These vectors were then summed by sex to provide the input for assessment (Table \@ref(tab:obsbio)). The full observed survey series for all three maturity definitions, together with total survey abundance, is listed in Table \@ref(tab:survey-series).  Input sample sizes are specified as 100 for both sexes and maturity states for all years of survey size composition data.

```{r obsbio, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
## Observed survey biomass with its sampling CV -- a checklist requirement
## ("survey biomass estimates with measures of uncertainty") and the target of
## the obsbio reference, which pointed at a table in an eval = FALSE chunk until
## 2026-08-29. Read from the model's own input file, so the table cannot drift
## from what was fitted. 2020 is absent because the survey was cancelled.
##
## Each biomass carries its CV in the same cell, and the 44 survey years run in
## two blocks side by side. Kept apart and stacked, the table was ten columns
## and three pages, which both overflowed the line and made flextable repeat its
## caption and label on every continuation page (backlog 9b).
.si_path <- "data/derived/survey_indices.csv"
if (file.exists(.si_path)) {
  .si <- read.csv(.si_path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  .cell <- function(b, cv) ifelse(is.na(b), "",
                                  sprintf("%.1f (%.2f)", b, cv))
  .mm <- .si[.si$sex == "male"   & .si$maturity == "mature", c("year","biomass","cv")]
  .mf <- .si[.si$sex == "female" & .si$maturity == "mature", c("year","biomass","cv")]
  .d  <- merge(.mm, .mf, by = "year", all = TRUE, suffixes = c(".m", ".f"))
  .d  <- .d[order(.d$year), ]
  stopifnot("survey_indices.csv should have no 2020 row (survey cancelled)" =
              !(2020 %in% .d$year))
  obsbio_df <- data.frame(
    Year   = as.character(.d$year),
    Male   = .cell(.d$biomass.m, .d$cv.m),
    Female = .cell(.d$biomass.f, .d$cv.f),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE)

  .n <- nrow(obsbio_df); .half <- ceiling(.n / 2)
  .a <- obsbio_df[seq_len(.half), ]
  .b <- obsbio_df[seq.int(.half + 1L, .n), ]
  if (nrow(.b) < nrow(.a)) .b[seq.int(nrow(.b) + 1L, nrow(.a)), ] <- ""
  names(.b) <- paste0(names(.b), " ")
  obsbio_df <- cbind(.a, .b); rownames(obsbio_df) <- NULL

  flextable::flextable(obsbio_df) |>
    flextable::fontsize(size = 8, part = "all") |>
    flextable::align(j = 2:5, align = "right", part = "all") |>
    ## Explicit widths (0.55 + 1.35 + 1.35 = 3.25 in per block, 6.3 in total,
    ## inside the 6.5 in portrait line). autofit() sized the six columns wider
    ## than the line, which pushed the right block off the page in Word and PDF
    ## and made the table look truncated at 2003 (fixed 2026-09-08).
    flextable::width(j = c(1, 4), width = 0.55) |>
    flextable::width(j = c(2, 3, 5, 6), width = 1.35) |>
    flextable::set_table_properties(layout = "fixed") |>
    flextable::padding(padding = 2, part = "all") |>
    ## Vertical rule between the two year blocks. Both reviewers and the author
    ## read the left block's last row (2003) as the end of the table, so the
    ## block boundary needs to be visible, not just described in the caption.
    flextable::vline(j = 3, border = officer::fp_border(color = "grey55", width = 1),
                     part = "all") |>
    flextable::set_caption(
      caption = paste("Observed mature male and mature female biomass at the time of the",
                      "NMFS summer survey (1,000 t), each followed by the coefficient of",
                      "variation of that estimate in parentheses. These are the survey",
                      "observations fitted by every model presented. Years run down the",
                      "left block and continue in the right. There is no 2020 row: the",
                      "survey was cancelled that year."),
      autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "obsbio")
    )
}
```



## Spatial distribution of survey abundance and catch
Snow crab are distributed widely over the eastern Bering Sea shelf, but their density and the extent of their distribution have changed over time (Zacher et al., 2026). Spatial gradients exist in the survey data by maturity and size for both sexes.  For example, larger males have been more prevalent on the southwest portion of the shelf while smaller males have been more prevalent on the northern portion of the shelf. Centroids of mature female abundance early in the history of the survey were farther south, but moved north during the 1990s. Since the late 1990s and early 2000s, the centroids moved south again, but not to the extent seen in the early 1980s. This phenomenon was mirrored in centroids of abundance for large males.

The observed distribution of large males during the summer survey and the fishery catch have historically differed, and the origin of this difference is unknown. It is possible that crab move between the fishery and the survey, but it is also possible that fishers do not target all portions of the distribution of large male crab equally. The underlying explanation of this phenomenon could hold implications for relative exploitation rates spatially and it has been suggested that high exploitation rates in the southern portion of the snow crab range may have resulted in a northward shift in snow crab distribution (Orensanz, 2004). Snow crab larvae likely drift north and east after hatching in spring. Snow crab appear to move south and west as they grow (Parada et al., 2010). However, little tagging data exists to fully characterize the ontogenetic or annual migration patterns of this stock (Murphy et al. 2010).

## Experimental study of survey selectivity

The Bering Sea Fisheries Research Foundation (BSFRF) has conducted supplementary surveys in the Bering Sea in which snow crab were caught during 2009, 2010, 2016, 2017, and 2018.  The location and extent of these surveys varied over the years as the survey goals changed. In 2009, the survey consisted of 108 tows around 27 survey stations and the goal was to improve understanding of snow crab densities and the selectivity of NMFS survey gear (Figure \@ref(fig:bsfrfmap)). Abundances estimated by the industry surveys were generally higher than the NMFS estimates, which suggests that the catchability of the NMFS survey gear is less than 1.

```{r bsfrfmap, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Location of the BSFRF survey selectivity experiments that provided data used in this assessment, over time."}
knitr::include_graphics("continuity/background/bsfrf_map.png")
```

In 2016, 2017, and 2018, snow crab were not the focus of the BSFRF surveys, but were still caught in the BSFRF gear. Comparing the ratio of the number of crab caught at length in the BSFRF gear (which is assumed to have a catchability/selectivity of 1 over all size classes) to the number of crab caught at length within the same area in the NMFS survey gear (which is assumed to have a catchability/selectivity <= 1 for at least some of the size classes) can provide an empirical estimate of catchability/selectivity (Figure \@ref(fig:bsfrf-sel)). Empirical estimates of catchability/selectivity vary by year and size class across the different BSFRF data sets (Figure \@ref(fig:bsfrf-sel-all) & Figure \@ref(fig:emp-sel)). The number of snow crab used to develop estimates of numbers at length likely contributes to these differences among years (Figure \@ref(fig:bsfrf-sampn)), but other factors may also influence catchability/selectivity at size of the NMFS survey gear (e.g. Somerton et al. 2013 show substrate type can influence selectivity). GAMs fit to the empirical estimates of selectivity are used as priors on estimated selectivity in the currently used assessment model. The standard errors from the GAMs are input as weighting factors for each prior of selectivity at size and sex derived from the BSFRF data.

```{r bsfrf-sel, echo=FALSE, out.width="89%", fig.cap="Observed numbers at length extrapolated from length-composition data and estimates of total numbers within the survey selectivity experimental areas, by year (left), and the inferred selectivity, the ratio of crab at length in the NMFS gear to that in the BSFRF gear (right)."}
knitr::include_graphics("continuity/background/BSFRF_NMFS_select.png")
```

```{r bsfrf-sel-all, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Inferred survey selectivity for all available years of BSFRF data."}
knitr::include_graphics("continuity/background/BSFRF_NMFS_select_allyrs.png")
```

```{r emp-sel, echo=FALSE, out.width="64%", fig.cap="Inferred selectivity from the BSFRF experiments with selectivity at size class estimated by a generalized additive model (top), and by a sample-size-weighted average (bottom)."}
knitr::include_graphics("continuity/background/avg_BSFRF_sel_alt.jpg")
```

```{r bsfrf-sampn, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Number of crab collected in the BSFRF experimental areas by the NMFS survey and by the BSFRF survey."}
knitr::include_graphics("continuity/background/sample_sizes.png")
```

# E. Analytic approach


## Model description

The Generalized Model for Assessing Crustacean Stocks (GMACS) was adopted as the assessment platform for snow crab in 2022 after a demonstration that GMACS could effectively reproduce the dynamics of the status quo model and offered structural improvements. GMACS is an integrated, size-structured model developed using automatic differentiation software developed as a set of libraries under C++ (ADModel Builder).  ADModel Builder can estimate a large number of parameters in a non-linear model using automatic differentiation software extended from Griewank and Corliss (1991) and developed into C++ class libraries.  GMACS version 2.20.34 was adopted for this assessment following the January 2026 CPT meeting and is used for every Tier 3 model presented. Newer GMACS releases have since superseded this version. It is retained here so that all models in this cycle are fit with the version the CPT reviewed.

The snow crab population dynamics model tracks the number of crab of sex *s*,  maturity state *m*, during year *y* at width *w*, N~*s,m,y,w*~. A terminal molt was modeled in which crab move from an immature to a mature state, after which no further molting occurred. The mid-points of the size bins tracked in the model spanned from 27.5 to 132.5 mm carapace width, with 5 mm size classes. The number of estimated parameters differs among the models: 407 in `Model 25.3`, `Model 26.1` and `Model 26.1a`, 412 in `Model 26.1b`, 386 in `Model 26.1c`, and 234 in `Model 26.2`. Parameters estimated within the assessment included those associated with the population processes recruitment, growth, natural mortality (subject to an informative prior and two years of additional 'mortality events' estimated in 2018 and 2019), fishing mortality, selectivity (fisheries and survey), and catchability. The yearly probability of undergoing terminal molt, weight at size, discard mortality, bycatch mortality, variance in growth increment, and parameters associated with proportion of recruitment allocated to size bin were estimated outside of the model or specified. The control files specifying the population dynamics are available from the GMACS repository linked in Section J.

A lognormal distribution was assumed for all catch and index time-series, while a robust multinomial was assumed for all size composition data. No likelihood weights were used in the assessment.

A 'jittering' approach has been historically used to explore the impact of different starting values on the assessment output (Turnock, 2016). Parameter values were jittered based on a normal distribution centered on one with a standard deviation of `r jit_fmt(jit_sd, 2)` that was then translated to the parameter space defined by the initial value and its bounds. `r if (jit_have) sprintf("%s jitters were run for the author-preferred model (Table \\@ref(tab:model-overview)); each run was started from an independently perturbed parameter vector and re-fit to convergence.", jit_n)` Each jitter run used an explicitly recorded random seed, so the analysis is exactly reproducible. The seed used by every run is stored alongside its results. Four of the six models presented were jittered (Table \@ref(tab:model-overview)). `Model 25.3` and `Model 26.1a` were not.

## Model selection and evaluation
Models were evaluated based on their fit to the data, evidence of non-convergence, the credibility of the estimated population processes, and the strength of the influence of the assumptions of the model on the outcomes of the assessment. Note that for some of the model scenarios, data inputs are different and, therefore, model fits are not directly comparable.

### Model summaries

The key assumptions of these models include: 

* the probability of terminally molting at size varies over time and size for males and is specified as fixed inputs to the model based on observations from the survey data. The female probability does not vary over time, which should be revisited

* survey selectivity is estimated by era (1982-88; 1989-present) and sex as a non-parametric curve subject to priors based on the BSFRF survey efficiency experiment data

* growth is a linear function of pre-molt carapace width with a specified variability around post-molt size

* all immature crab molt

* natural mortality is estimated by sex and maturity state with additional mortality events estimated in 2018 and 2019 and subject to a prior based on an assumed longevity of 20 years

* total and retained fishery selectivity are estimated logistic curves

* all non-directed bycatch (e.g. snow crab caught in the Tanner crab fishery or crab caught in the non-pelagic trawl fisheries) is lumped into a single 'fishery' for which a single selectivity is estimated. These removals are recorded for both sexes combined, so in the male-only sensitivity they are fit by the male population alone and the bycatch fishing mortality estimated for males is correspondingly inflated (the affected removals average 0.48 kt against a mean retained catch of 37.1 kt, and the fit to the series is essentially unchanged)

* recruitment is estimated separately for females and males and is allocated in the first 3 size bins. The male-only sensitivity estimates male recruitment only


### Model scenarios

#### Model numbering and its correspondence with the May 2026 assessment {-}

The models presented here are numbered on the 2026 cycle, following the May 2026 Crab Plan Team report, which noted that the 2025 accepted model had been mistakenly labeled `Model 25` in the preliminary assessment (its accepted number is `Model 25.3`) and that the runs introduced in May 2026 had been mistakenly numbered on the 2025 cycle. The review guidelines distinguish major changes, which take a new integer, from minor ones, which take a letter. A change to the data alone is treated here as minor. Because the June 2026 SSC report refers to the configuration accepted in May by its May number, the full correspondence is given below.

| This document | May 2026 preliminary assessment | Terminal year | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| Model 25.3 | Model 25 | 2024 | 2025 accepted assessment, rolled forward |
| **Model 26.1** | **Model 25.2c** | 2024 | Configuration accepted by the CPT in May 2026 |
| Model 26.1a | Model 25.2e | 2024 | 26.1 with the binning and growth-data corrections |
| **Model 26.1b** | Model 25.2e (new data) | 2025 | **Author-preferred**: 26.1a with the 2025 fishery and 2026 survey |
| Model 26.1c | Model 25.2e (2019 data) | 2019 | 26.1b truncated to 2019, convergence diagnostic |
| Model 26.2 | Model 26.1 | 2025 | 26.1b with the female population removed |

The configuration the June 2026 SSC report calls `Model 25.2c` is `Model 26.1` here, and the author-preferred run, `Model 26.1b`, is that same configuration with the two data corrections and a further year of data.

#### The models {-}

A total of `r n_models` models were explored (Table \@ref(tab:model-overview)). All models share the same structural assumptions described above and differ only in the version of GMACS and their data inputs. The one exception is `Model 26.2`, which removes the female population entirely and is therefore a structural change. The naming convention reflects an additive series of changes layered onto the September 2025 model (`Model 25.3`). 

The base ('rolled forward') model:

* **Model 25.3**: the September 2025 author-preferred model, included for reference only. No data are updated and no structural changes are made. It was fitted under an earlier version of GMACS and is reported as originally fitted.

Models brought forward from the May 2026 assessment:

* **Model 26.1**: the model accepted by the CPT in May 2026. `Model 25.3` updated to GMACS 2.20.34, with the total-male size composition corrected and the plus group enlarged to include all crab greater than 135 mm carapace width, and with the molting probability controls replaced by the new maturity workflow developed by the Kodiak lab (E. Ryznar, in prep). That workflow fits an `sdmTMB` spatiotemporal model to chela-based maturity classifications to produce a smoothed probability of being mature at size and location, integrated to a population-level annual ogive. The updated series shows a weaker temporal trend in the probability of terminal molt at intermediate sizes. As in May, the model includes fishery data through the 2023/24 season and survey data through the 2024 survey.

* **Model 26.1a**: as `Model 26.1`, but with the size-composition bin convention changed so that a crab falling exactly on a 5 mm cutoff is assigned to the upper bin, and with a transcription error in the growth data corrected (a 26.3 mm crab's molt increment recorded as 73 mm where the specimen master gives 7.3 mm). Fishery data run through the 2023/24 season and survey data through the 2024 survey. Presented to isolate the effect of the two data corrections against the May baseline.

The September 2026 models:

* **Model 26.1b**: the author-preferred model. The `Model 26.1a` configuration with one more year of data: fishery data through the 2025/26 season and survey data through the 2026 summer survey. The data are updated. The model is not.

* **Model 26.1c**: the same configuration with fishery data ending at the 2019/20 season and survey data ending at the 2019 summer survey. Requested by the CPT in May 2026 to test whether the convergence problems originate in estimating recruitment following the 2018-19 collapse and across the 2020 survey gap. The estimated parameter count is 386.

Sensitivity to the female data and dynamics:

* **Model 26.2**: `Model 26.1b` with the female population removed entirely, not down-weighted. The number of sexes is set to one, which removes the female size compositions, the female survey indices, the female discard catch, and the female growth observations from the data, and removes the female recruitment, natural mortality, growth, and selectivity parameters from the model. The estimated parameter count falls from 412 to 234. Fixing the female estimation phases alone would be insufficient: a combined-sex catch observation is predicted by summing over both sexes, and the recruitment scale and deviations are not sex-specific, so the female population would continue to influence fishing mortality and recruitment. The non-directed bycatch is recorded for both sexes combined and is therefore fit by the male population alone in this run, as noted among the assumptions above. This is the only model presented here that differs structurally from `Model 26.1a`, so it takes a new number instead of a parenthetical. Requested by the CPT in May 2026 and presented as a sensitivity only. Like every other model here it is not proposed for the 2026/27 specification.

The May 2026 preliminary assessment presented a bracket of fourteen candidate models exploring three axes of uncertainty: the treatment of *Chionoecetes* hybrids, the new maturity workflow, and a set of attempts to improve convergence by correcting the total-male composition, expanding the plus group, and adding an immature survey index. That bracket is not repeated here. The CPT and SSC concluded that hybrid catch and survey data should not be included in the assessment model at this time, and agreed that the immature survey index should not be treated as a convergence fix, so neither the hybrid nor the immature-index candidates are brought forward. The composition correction and the expanded plus group, which the SSC supported as clear technical improvements, are incorporated in every model presented above. The full May bracket and its results remain available in the May 2026 preliminary assessment document.

Time series of data used in the assessment are visualized in Figures \@ref(fig:indexdataplots), \@ref(fig:catchdataplots) and \@ref(fig:compdataplots).

## Results
### Model convergence and comparison
All `r n_models` models presented here inverted their Hessians (Table \@ref(tab:max-grad)). Every fit was improved by including additional Newton steps, including the two that already met the conventional threshold of a maximum absolute gradient < 0.001, so the set is treated consistently. Newton steps reduced the gradient without moving the fit: across the models they changed the objective function and the management quantities by less than 0.0001 percent (the largest movement was in `Model 26.1c`). `Model 25.3`, which was fitted under an earlier version of GMACS and cannot be re-run with the current executable, is reported as originally fitted and retains a maximum gradient of 0.00134. Likelihood components by category for each model are summarized in Tables \@ref(tab:like-index-tot), \@ref(tab:like-comp-tot), and \@ref(tab:like-other-tot).

A zero gradient indicates that the fit is at a stationary point of the likelihood. It does not indicate that the parameters are well determined or that other stationary points do not exist.

`r if (!jit_have) "*Jitter results not yet generated; run 05_run_jitter.R to produce them. The paragraphs below will populate from those runs.*"`

As in past cycles, jittering was used to evaluate sensitivity to starting values. The results reported in this section are for `Model 26.1b`. Results for the other jittered models are given in Appendix B. `r if (jit_have) sprintf("Of the %s runs, %s produced a complete set of estimates and %s attained a maximum absolute gradient below %s. %s of the runs met the conventional threshold of %s. For comparison, the accepted fit attained %s before Newton steps and reports a maximum gradient of zero after them (Table \\@ref(tab:max-grad)); the jitter runs are reported on their gradients before Newton steps, making them comparable with one another.", jit_fmt(jit_n,0), jit_fmt(jit_complete,0), jit_fmt(jit_conv,0), format(jit_man$grad_usable), jit_fmt(.js('n_meets_conventional'),0), format(jit_man$grad_conventional), trimws(formatC(.js('base_max_grad'), format='g', digits=3)))`

The practical cost of the multiple minima is visible in `Model 26.1`. The jitter analysis located a solution 1.27 negative log-likelihood units better than the fit obtained from the model's own starting values, a difference that would ordinarily be considered small. Adopting it moved B~MSY~ by less than one percent, but moved the total OFL from 50.27 to 43.83 kt. The total OFL here is OFL(tot) from `Gmacsall.out`, which is retained catch plus discard mortality summed over all fleets, not the retained-only quantity `spr_cofl_ret`. The choice among solutions that the data separate only weakly therefore has more effect on the management quantities than several of the structural choices examined in this assessment.

`r if (jit_have && jit_multimodal) sprintf("The runs converged to %d distinct minima (Figure \\@ref(fig:jitter)), confirming that the multimodality reported in the 2025 preliminary and final assessments persists in the 2026 model. The largest cluster of solutions accounted for %s%% of the runs that reached a minimum, but that cluster is not the best fit: the solution adopted here was reached by only %s of them. Across all runs, the directed OFL ranged from %s to %s kt and mature male biomass in %s ranged from %s to %s kt, so the choice of starting values, not the data, moves the management quantities across that range. The same separation is visible in male recruitment (Figure \\@ref(fig:jitt-rec)) and in MMB (Figure \\@ref(fig:jitt-ssb)).", jit_nmodes, jit_fmt(jit_pct_best,1), jit_fmt(jit_n_at_base,0), jit_fmt(jit_ofl_min,2), jit_fmt(jit_ofl_max,2), jit_fmt(jit_term_yr,0), jit_fmt(jit_mmb_min,1), jit_fmt(jit_mmb_max,1))`
`r if (jit_have && !jit_multimodal) sprintf("The runs converged to a single minimum (Figure \\@ref(fig:jitter)); the multimodality reported in the 2025 preliminary and final assessments is not evident in the 2026 model. The directed OFL across the runs ranged from %s to %s kt and mature male biomass in %s from %s to %s kt, which is the residual spread within one minimum, not a separation between minima.", jit_fmt(jit_ofl_min,2), jit_fmt(jit_ofl_max,2), jit_fmt(jit_term_yr,0), jit_fmt(jit_mmb_min,1), jit_fmt(jit_mmb_max,1))`

`r if (jit_have && jit_improve > 0.001 && jit_promoted) sprintf("One jitter run found a better fit than the starting solution, improving the negative log likelihood by %s units. Following the convention used in the 2025 assessment, that run was adopted as the reported model and re-fit with the Hessian; all quantities reported derive from it. The provenance of that fit, including its random seed, is recorded with the model.", jit_fmt(jit_improve,3))`
`r if (jit_have && jit_improve > 0.001 && !jit_promoted) sprintf("One jitter run found a better fit than the reported model, improving the negative log likelihood by %s units. It has not been adopted.", jit_fmt(jit_improve,3))`
`r if (jit_have && jit_improve <= 0.001) "No jitter run improved materially on the reported fit, which supports the reported solution being the global minimum, not a local one."`

`r if (jit_have && !is.null(jitter$attribution)) sprintf("The parameters that separate the minima are summarized in Table \\@ref(tab:jitter-attribution) and Figure \\@ref(fig:jitt-attrib). Identifying which parameters differ between the minima, rather than only observing that they exist, was requested by the SSC and is intended to direct the structural work needed to resolve the multiple minima.")` Differences in multiple parameters resulted in local minima, making a quick solution to the convergence problems challenging. Natural mortality, recruitment, and initial numbers at size all vary considerably among the minima.

Removing the female population improves the numerical behavior of the model. `Model 26.2` estimates 234 parameters compared with 412 for `Model 26.1b`. Its accepted fit attains a maximum absolute gradient of zero to reported precision after additional Newton steps, and its Hessian is markedly better conditioned than that of `Model 26.1b` (condition number 3.3e05 compared with 1.4e06; smallest eigenvalue 120 compared with 35), with no non-positive eigenvalues. The condition number is the ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue of the Hessian. A smaller value indicates a better-determined minimum, and very large values indicate near-flat directions in the likelihood along which the parameters are poorly determined. Jittering the male-only model over 100 runs recovered its accepted fit in `r .f(jit_mo_pct, 1)` percent of the runs that reached a minimum, compared with `r .f(jit_pct_at_base, 1)` percent for `Model 26.1b`, so dropping the females reduced, but did not remove, the multimodality that has characterized this assessment. The retrospective pattern is also smaller: Mohn's rho for mature male biomass is -0.09 (-0.08 when the terminal survey year is withheld) compared with -0.11 for `Model 26.1b`, and both remain inside the Hurtado-Ferro et al. (2015) bounds. Mohn's rho for male recruitment falls from approximately 8 to 0.7. These improvements are consistent with removing the females reducing the confounding among growth, natural mortality, and selectivity.

One caveat applies. In `Model 26.2` the base natural mortality offset for immature males is estimated at its lower bound of -1, with a standard error of 2e-05. Because M is specified as relative for that group, the bound puts immature-male M at exp(-1) times the mature-male rate, or 0.106 yr^-1^. The same parameter in the accepted two-sex model is estimated at -0.225 with a standard error of 0.117, well inside its range, giving 0.232 yr^-1^. Removing the females results in the model estimating immature-male mortality at about a third of the mature rate, and the estimate would go lower if allowed. Because that parameter is pinned at its bound, it no longer contributes a direction of uncertainty to the Hessian, so part of the improvement in conditioning reflects the bound rather than a better-determined likelihood. The implied immature-male mortality should also not be adopted in a specification model without further examination. The other parameters at bounds in `Model 26.2` are the three fully-selected trawl-survey size classes, which are at bounds in the two-sex model as well and are not diagnostic. Dropping the females also lowers the reference points: $B_{MSY}$ falls from 144.97 to 131.34 kt, the total-catch OFL from 85.65 to 77.00 kt, and terminal mature male biomass from 141.53 to 115.90 kt (Table \@ref(tab:stepchange)).

```{r jitter-attribution, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F}
# Parameters separating the jitter clouds. Present only when the runs settled
# into more than one optimum -- with a single optimum there is nothing to
# attribute, and the chunk emits nothing rather than an empty table.
if (jit_have && !is.null(jitter$attribution)) {
  # Top 10 of the 15 rows the attribution returns. The table is a ranking, so a
  # top-N is the natural presentation, and at 15 rows it broke across a page --
  # which makes flextable repeat the caption AND the label (backlog 9b).
  N_ATTRIB <- 10L
  jattr_df <- utils::head(jitter$attribution, N_ATTRIB)
  ## Human-readable name for each GMACS parameter block, requested by GA review
  ## 2026-08-31: "T_pars, G_pars, etc are not easily interpreted". Prefix map,
  ## consistent with the "What it is" column of Table \@ref(tab:max-grad).
  .attr_desc <- function(x) {
    dplyr::case_when(
      grepl("^logit_rec_prop", x) ~ "recruitment sex allocation",
      grepl("^T_pars",  x) ~ "recruitment scale / initial numbers at size",
      grepl("^M_pars",  x) ~ "natural mortality",
      grepl("^S_pars|^Sel", x) ~ "selectivity",
      grepl("^G_pars",  x) ~ "growth",
      grepl("^F_pars|^log_fbar|^log_fdev", x) ~ "fishing mortality",
      grepl("^rec_dev|^Rec", x) ~ "recruitment deviations",
      grepl("^Initial_logN|^logN", x) ~ "initial numbers at size",
      TRUE ~ ""
    )
  }
  jattr_df <- data.frame(
    Parameter  = jattr_df$parameter,
    `What it is` = .attr_desc(jattr_df$parameter),
    Comparison = paste0(jattr_df$mode_a, " vs ", jattr_df$mode_b),
    `Mean in A` = round(jattr_df$mean_a, 4),
    `Mean in B` = round(jattr_df$mean_b, 4),
    Difference = round(jattr_df$difference, 4),
    `Std. difference` = round(jattr_df$std_difference, 2),
    check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

  flextable::flextable(jattr_df) |>
  # Long table, breaks across a page. Suppress the repeated caption in the
  # longtable continuation head -- it repeats the \label with it and makes
  # \@ref(tab:jitter-attribution) ambiguous (2026-08-30).
  flextable::set_table_properties(opts_pdf = list(caption_repeat = FALSE)) |>
    flextable::fontsize(size = 8, part = "all") |>
    flextable::autofit() |>
    ## Rescale to the 6.5 in portrait line; autofit alone sized this table
    ## wider than the page and clipped the right-hand columns (2026-09-08).
    flextable::fit_to_width(max_width = 6.4) |>
    flextable::set_caption(
      caption = sprintf(paste("The %d parameter differences that most separate pairs of jitter",
                              "minima in Model 26.1b, ranked by the standardized difference in",
                              "fitted value. Each row compares the two minima named in the",
                              "Comparison column. The minima compared differ among rows.",
                              "Parameter values are in the units of the estimated parameter",
                              "(log scale for most blocks). The standardized difference is",
                              "dimensionless."),
                        nrow(jattr_df)),
      autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "jitter-attribution")
    )
}
