```{r retro-setup, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Retrospective outputs, written by 06_run_retrospective.R. Every value quoted
# in the narrative below is pulled from these files at knit time so the text
# cannot drift from the runs.
# Follow the accepted model rather than naming a folder. Hardcoded, this would
# report a DIFFERENT model's retrospective without warning if accepted_model
# were repointed -- which it was on 2026-08-28 (see the note above).
retro_dir <- file.path(report_model, "retro")
stopifnot("retro_dir does not exist for the accepted model" = dir.exists(retro_dir))

.rd <- function(f) {
  p <- file.path(retro_dir, f)
  if (file.exists(p)) read.csv(p, stringsAsFactors = FALSE) else NULL
}
retro_rho  <- .rd("mohns_rho.csv")
retro_rel  <- .rd("retro_peel_relative.csv")
retro_diag <- .rd("retro_diagnostics.csv")
# The retrospective reports MMB and recruitment only. There is no
# retro_refpoints.csv: GMACS does not compute reference points for a peeled run
# (gmacsbase.TPL 2.20.34 gates both call sites on nyrRetroNo == 0, :5478 and
# :13625), so every peel returns them as exactly 0. Confirmed 2026-08-27; the
# peels run WITH the Hessian, so this was never a -nohess problem. The terminal
# fit's reference points are in the model directory and retro/base_run.csv.
#
# NOT read here: retro/prj_growth_year_diagnostic.csv. It is a developer
# diagnostic, not an assessment result, and its BMSY = OFL = 0 columns are that
# same peel behavior. Nothing in the SAFE should be able to reach those zeros.

retro_have <- !is.null(retro_rho)

# convenience accessors; return NA (not an error) when the runs are absent
.rho <- function(mode, quantity) {
  if (!retro_have) return(NA_real_)
  v <- retro_rho$mohns_rho[retro_rho$mode == mode & retro_rho$quantity == quantity]
  if (length(v)) v[1] else NA_real_
}
.fmt <- function(x, d = 3) if (is.na(x)) "NA" else formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)

retro_npeel <- if (!is.null(retro_rel)) max(retro_rel$peel) else NA_integer_
retro_yr1   <- if (!is.null(retro_rel)) max(retro_rel$terminal_year) else NA_integer_
retro_yrN   <- if (!is.null(retro_rel)) min(retro_rel$terminal_year) else NA_integer_

## Mohn's rho for EVERY model given a retrospective sweep this cycle -- the four
## jittered models, each of which has retro/mohns_rho.csv in its folder. Keyed
## off model_defs and model_jittered so a renamed or repointed folder cannot be
## mislabeled; a model whose sweep has not been run simply drops out of the
## table rather than appearing as a blank row.
.retro_set <- names(model_defs)[model_jittered[names(model_defs)] == "Y"]
retro_all <- do.call(rbind, lapply(.retro_set, function(nm) {
  p <- file.path(model_defs[[nm]], "retro", "mohns_rho.csv")
  if (!file.exists(p)) return(NULL)
  cbind(Model = as.character(to_short(nm)),
        read.csv(p, stringsAsFactors = FALSE), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
if (!is.null(retro_all)) retro_all <- retro_all[order(retro_all$Model), ]
```

The guidelines also ask whether any parameters were inestimable or reached their bounds. No parameter reached a bound in the accepted fit of `Model 26.1b`, and its Hessian is well conditioned: its smallest eigenvalue is 34.6, and none is non-positive. Twenty-four of the 412 estimated parameters have a standard error larger than the absolute value of the estimate. Sixteen of those are estimated within 0.1 of zero, where a large ratio is expected rather than diagnostic: four selectivity offsets, three fishing mortality deviations, two fishing mortality offsets, two recruitment deviations, three recruitment proportion parameters, one growth parameter, and one natural mortality parameter, `M_pars_est[10]`, estimated at 0.022 with a standard error of 0.84. That last parameter is near zero but poorly determined, so it raises an identifiability question. The remainder are three recruitment deviations, three recruitment proportion parameters, a fishing mortality deviation, and `M_pars_est[2]`, the natural mortality deviation for mature males in the first event block, estimated at 0.33 with a standard error of 0.59.

These results describe the accepted fit of `Model 26.1b`, not every fit of that model. When the model is started from its default initial values rather than from a previously identified solution, it can settle in a minimum where the 2019 immature-female natural mortality deviation, `M_pars_est[15]`, is not identified: the estimate drifts toward its upper bound of 10 with a standard error of order 5 x 10^3^, and the smallest Hessian eigenvalue falls to 1.1 x 10^-6^. In the accepted fit the same parameter is estimated at 1.83 with a standard error of 0.58, consistent with the 2018 deviation for the same group (1.80). Whether an exponential time-varying natural mortality block on immature females is identifiable from these data is a question for the Plan Team. The alternative is to fix it, as the corresponding rows for the other sex and maturity combinations already are.

### Retrospective analysis
`r if (!retro_have) "*Retrospective results not yet generated; run 06_run_retrospective.R to produce them.*"`

Retrospective analyses were performed by sequentially removing the terminal year of data from the model, re-fitting, and comparing the resulting time series of estimated mature male biomass with the estimates from the model fit to the full data set. A retrospective pattern is a consistent directional change in an assessment estimate for a given year as additional years of data are added. `r if (retro_have) sprintf("A total of %d retrospective model runs (peels) were made, giving terminal years from %d to %d.", retro_npeel, retro_yr1, retro_yrN)` The peels did not meet the maximum-gradient criterion of 0.001 applied to the accepted fit; the maximum absolute gradient ranged from 0.0015 to 0.020. Each peel is near a local minimum and none received additional Newton steps.

Mohn's $\rho$ is reported here as the mean across peels of the relative difference between each peel's terminal-year estimate and the estimate for that same year from the model fit to all of the data,

$$\rho = \frac{1}{P}\sum_{p=1}^{P}\frac{X_{T_p,\,p}-X_{T_p,\,0}}{X_{T_p,\,0}},$$

where $T_p$ is the terminal year of peel $p$ and $X_{\cdot,0}$ is the unpeeled fit. A positive $\rho$ means the peels sit above the full model, i.e. that terminal biomass is revised downward as data accumulate. Hurtado-Ferro et al. (2015) suggest that $\rho$ outside $[-0.22,\,0.30]$ for a short-lived stock indicates a retrospective pattern worth reporting.

Two retrospective analyses are presented. First, the standard retrospective removes the last $p$ years of all data streams, including the survey. Because an assessment with fishery data through season $N$ includes the summer survey from year $N+1$, each standard peel still retains one survey year beyond its terminal fishery season. Second, the dropped-terminal-survey retrospective also withholds that final survey year, isolating the influence of the single most recent survey observation on the terminal estimate.

`r if (retro_have) sprintf("For mature male biomass in Model 26.1b, the standard retrospective gave Mohn's $\\rho$ = %s and the dropped-terminal-survey retrospective gave $\\rho$ = %s (Table \\@ref(tab:retro-rho), Figures \\@ref(fig:retro-mmb) and \\@ref(fig:retro-drop-survey)). Male recruitment gave $\\rho$ = %s.", .fmt(.rho("standard","mature_male_biomass")), .fmt(.rho("drop_survey","mature_male_biomass")), .fmt(.rho("standard","recruitment_male")))`

Retrospectives were also run for the other three jittered models, and Table \@ref(tab:retro-rho) reports all four. For mature male biomass, Mohn's $\rho$ lies inside the Hurtado-Ferro et al. (2015) bounds for every model, ranging from -0.20 (`Model 26.1`, terminal survey dropped) to 0.07 (`Model 26.1c`). For male recruitment it exceeds the bounds in every model, ranging from 0.68 (`Model 26.2`) to 9.51 (`Model 26.1b`, terminal survey dropped), so terminal recruitment estimates are unreliable in every configuration and least so in the male-only model.

Management quantities are not recomputed for each peel. GMACS calculates reference points only when the retrospective peel count is zero (`gmacsbase.TPL` 2.20.34 gates both call sites on `nyrRetroNo == 0`), so every peeled run returns $B_{MSY}$, $B/B_{MSY}$ and the OFL as exactly zero rather than as estimates. This is a property of GMACS, not of the runs presented here, and it applies equally to the 2025 assessment. The retrospective therefore characterizes only mature male biomass and recruitment.

The mature male biomass pattern is modest. In `Model 26.1b` the peels sit below the full model, so terminal biomass has tended to be revised upward as data accumulated. These retrospectives are of the Tier 3 models. The 2026/27 specification is calculated under Tier 4 from the REMA-smoothed survey series, so they have little bearing on the ABC buffer recommended here.

### Historical analysis

The retrospective analysis above withholds data from a single model. A historical analysis asks how the perception of the stock has changed across successive assessments accepted for management. Figure \@ref(fig:historical-mmb) shows estimated mature male biomass at mating from each assessment from 2016 to 2025.

The revisions are much larger than the within-model retrospective pattern. The 2020 assessment estimated 2020 mature male biomass at the time of the survey at 486.5 kt. The 2021 assessment, with the 2021 survey, revised that year to 40.95 kt, a 92 percent reduction. The revision then reversed: at the time of mating, the 2022 assessment estimated 2020 biomass at 19.1 kt and the 2023 assessment revised the same year to 205.4 kt. Terminal-year estimates across the ten assessments range from 26.7 kt (2021 assessment) to 207.2 kt (2020 assessment). The main drivers of these revisions were changes in the treatment of terminal molt and of the BSFRF selectivity priors, changes in the definition of mature male biomass used, and the absence of a 2020 survey.

The practical consequence for management advice is that terminal-year mature male biomass in this assessment has historically been revised by considerably more than the within-model retrospective analysis implies, and in both directions. All series in Figure \@ref(fig:historical-mmb) are from the Tier 3 assessments accepted in each year and are shown as absolute mature male biomass without normalization. Uncertainty intervals for the historical estimates are available in the archived model files and could be added to this figure in a future cycle.

```{r historical-mmb, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Estimated mature male biomass at mating (1,000 t) as seen by each Tier 3 assessment accepted for management from 2016 to 2025, against the current assessment. The top panel is biomass at the time of the survey and the bottom panel is biomass at mating. Values are point estimates only, without uncertainty intervals."}
knitr::include_graphics("plots/historical_mating_mmb_est.png")
```

### Model fits
Fits to the survey indices of mature biomass were broadly similar across the models (Figure \@ref(fig:mmbfits)). `Model 26.1b`, the only two-sex model that includes the 2026 survey, continues to have difficulty fitting the terminal year of female biomass. `Model 26.2` estimates no female population, so the issue does not arise for it. The yearly varying probability of terminal molt from the new maturity workflow, used by every model other than `Model 25.3`, shifts the estimated population dynamics modestly but does not resolve the female terminal-year fit (Figure \@ref(fig:mmbfits)).

Fits to the non-directed fishery catches were good for all models (Figure \@ref(fig:catchfits)). Fits to the directed-fishery retained catch were also good across the model set.
Differences among models in the fits to size composition data for retained catch in the directed fishery are small (size composition figures, below). No visually discernible differences among models existed for female discards from the directed fishery. Fits to the non-directed fishery had some of the largest misfits of all data sources (particularly for male data), but this is expected given a single estimated selectivity curve and changes in fishery behavior over time. Input sample sizes are assumed to be 100 for all composition data except for female discards in 2021, 2024 and 2025 (input sample size = 10). Actual numbers of crab measured are far larger, so the input value caps the weight given to each composition. Year-specific input sample sizes are a possible future refinement.

Fits to the survey size composition data were broadly similar across models in most years (size composition figures, below). All models had difficulty fitting the size composition data for immature females in 2009 and 2019, which could suggest some unmodeled size-based mortality or time-varying probability of terminal molt. Estimates of mean growth are shown in Figure \@ref(fig:growthfits).

### Estimated population processes

The estimates in this section are from the Tier 3 models, which do not converge reliably (Section E, Appendix B). Inference from these estimates should therefore be treated with caution.

The estimated abundance of commercially preferred male crab (> 101 mm carapace width) varied among models (Figure \@ref(fig:obs-101-vs-pred)). Annual estimates of mature biomass and preferred-male abundance from Model 26.1b, both at the survey and for the whole population, are listed in Table \@ref(tab:predsurvbio), and total numbers of crab in Table \@ref(tab:predtotnum). The early years when differences in survey selectivity occurred were particularly variable. All models agreed that the abundance in recent years has been the lowest in the time series (Figure \@ref(fig:obs-101-vs-pred-bio)). The estimates of the most recent era of survey selectivity were similar across models for both sexes (Figure \@ref(fig:select-prior)).

Estimated fisheries selectivities were similar across models (Figure \@ref(fig:predselectfish)). Estimated fully-selected fishing mortality for the directed fishery was highly variable and relatively high for most of the fishery history (Figure \@ref(fig:predfmort)). The total fishery selectivity curve is shifted far to the right, so only the largest crab experience the fully-selected fishing mortality. 

The probability of undergoing terminal molt is input as data (Figure \@ref(fig:predmat)). The status quo workflow produces a strong increasing trend through time at intermediate sizes (e.g., at 77 mm the probability rose from ~0.2 in the early 1990s to ~0.5 after 2010), while the new maturity workflow produces a much weaker temporal trend (~0.35 to 0.45 throughout the time series). The new workflow uses a spatiotemporal `sdmTMB` model fit to chela-based maturity classifications and borrows information across years and locations for size bins with sparse chela data. It does not extrapolate the predicted spatial probability surface beyond stations with measured crab.

Trends in recruitment were very similar across models for the early time series, with some variability in scale and differences in timing between the sexes (Figure \@ref(fig:recruits)). The male and female series are not independent. GMACS estimates a single annual total recruitment and allocates it between the sexes with an estimated annual logit-scale proportion parameter, so a difference in timing between the sexes reflects the estimated allocation, not separate recruitment processes. Differences in estimated recruitment in the most recent years were observed among models for males and contribute to differences in OFLs across the model set.

Base estimates of natural mortality for mature animals of both sexes were broadly similar across the models presented (Figure \@ref(fig:nat-m), Table \@ref(tab:stepchange)). All models estimated additional mortality events that removed a large fraction of crab by sex and maturity state, except for mature females, at some point during the marine heatwave of 2018-19. In some of the alternative minima found by the jitter analysis, the immature-female natural mortality deviation for the second event block is poorly determined, with a standard error far larger than the estimate. In the preferred model (`Model 26.1b`) it is not, as reported under model convergence, where whether it should be fixed rather than estimated is also discussed.

### MMB and management quantities
Estimated mature male biomass time series had similar trends across models but differed in scale (Figure \@ref(fig:predmmb)). Annual MMB, male recruitment and directed-fishery fishing mortality for the reference and accepted models are listed in Table \@ref(tab:predsurvbio-tot). Estimates of $B_{MSY}$, current MMB relative to $B_{MSY}$, $F_{MSY}$, $F_{OFL}$ and the Tier 3 OFL are summarized in Table \@ref(tab:stepchange). Across the models presented, the $B_{MSY}$ proxy ranged from 131.3 to 180.1 kt and terminal mature male biomass from 86.9 to 141.5 kt. The three models whose data end in 2024 place the stock below its $B_{MSY}$ proxy (status 0.81 to 0.96), while the two that include the 2025 fishery and 2026 survey place it above (status 1.23 and 1.32). The additional year of data, rather than any structural change, accounts for that difference. `Model 26.1c`, whose data end in 2019, sits just above the proxy at 1.05, but its reference points are computed from a different span of data and are not comparable with the others.

# F. Calculation of the OFL
## Methodology for OFL 
### Tier 3
Historically, the Tier 3 OFL was calculated using proxies for biomass and fishing mortality reference points and a sloped control rule. Proxies for biomass and fishing mortality reference points were calculated using spawning-biomass-per-recruit methods (e.g. Clark, 1991). After fitting the assessment model to the data and estimating population parameters, the model was projected forward 100 years using the estimated parameters under no exploitation and constant recruitment to determine 'unfished' mature male biomass-per-recruit. Projections were repeated in which the bisection method was used to identify a fishing mortality that reduced the mature male biomass-per-recruit to 35% of the unfished level (i.e. F~35%~ and B~35%~). Calculations of F~*35%*~ were made under the assumption that bycatch fishing mortality was equal to the estimated average value over the last 10 years. 

Calculated values of F~35%~ and B~35%~ were used in conjunction with a Tier 3 control rule to adjust the proportion of F~35%~ that is applied to the stock based on the status of the population relative to B~35%~ (Amendment 24, NMFS). To determine the F~OFL~, the population is projected to the time of fishing for the upcoming fishery under no fishing. If the MMB at that time exceeds 25% of B~35%~, a fishery can occur and the F~OFL~ is calculated as:

$$\begin{equation}
F_{OFL} =
\begin{cases}
Bycatch  & if \frac{MMB}{B_{35}} \leq 0.25 \\[3ex]
\frac {F_{35} ( \frac {MMB}{B_{35}} - \alpha)}{1-\alpha}  & if 0.25 < \frac {MMB}{B_{35}} < 1 \\[3ex]
F_{35} & if MMB > B_{35}
\end{cases}
\end{equation}$$

Where MMB is the projected morphometrically mature male biomass in the current survey year after fishing at the F~*OFL*~, B~*35%*~ is the mature male biomass at the time of mating resulting from fishing at F~*35%*~, F~*35%*~ is the fishing mortality that reduces the morphometrically mature male biomass per recruit to 35% of unfished levels, and $\alpha$ determines the slope of the descending limb of the harvest control rule (set to 0.1 here).

Calculated total Tier 3 OFLs across the models presented ranged from 43.8 to 147.3 kt (Table \@ref(tab:stepchange)). For reference, the observed biomass of morphometrically mature males in the 2025 survey was `r .f(survey_morph_2025, 1)` kt and of preferred males (> 101 mm) `r .f(survey_pref_2025, 1)` kt. The model accepted in May, `Model 26.1`, gives an OFL of 43.8 kt. Correcting the size-composition bin convention and the growth transcription error (`Model 26.1a`) lowered the $B_{MSY}$ proxy from 172.7 to 158.7 kt and raised the OFL to 53.7 kt. Adding the 2025 fishery and 2026 survey (`Model 26.1b`) lowered the proxy further to 145.0 kt, raised status above one, and raised the OFL to 85.6 kt. The male-only sensitivity gives a lower OFL than the model it is derived from (77.0 kt compared with 85.6 kt). The run truncated to 2019 is not comparable with the others because its reference points are computed from a different span of data.

### Tier 4

The Tier 4 model is the basis for the 2026 harvest specification. The SSC assigned this stock to Tier 4b when it set the 2025/26 specification (October 2025 SSC report, Table 2), and that subtier is used here. A random-effects model (REMA) is fitted to the observed survey biomass series, the B~MSY~ proxy is the mean of the smoothed series, and stock status is the terminal smoothed biomass relative to that proxy. Target fishing mortality is F = M = `r .f(NAT_M, 2)` yr^-1^, the median of the prior on natural mortality.

The averaging period for the B~MSY~ proxy is the full survey time series, `r .fy(BMSY_WINDOW_LAB)`. The proxy represents the long-term average productivity of the stock, so the most recent observation is included. The September 2025 assessment averaged 1982 to 2024 and omitted the terminal year. The average is taken over the smoothed series rather than the observations because the smoothed series supplies a value for 2020, when the survey was cancelled. The smoothed series, with its prediction intervals, is listed by maturity definition in Table \@ref(tab:rema-series).

The choice of averaging window affects the reference points and, through stock status, the recommended OFL. Recomputing this cycle's smoothed series on the narrower 1982 to 2024 window gives a B~MSY~ proxy of 148.18 kt and a status of 0.769, compared with `r .f(bmsy_2026, 2)` kt and `r .f(status_2026, 3)` on the full window. The effect of the window choice is small, about 1 percent on both the proxy and the OFL. The flat-rule sensitivity (F = M applied to the terminal biomass) does not depend on the proxy and is unchanged by the choice of window.

Three definitions of mature male biomass are reported, as in the September 2025 assessment: morphometrically mature males, large males (>= 95 mm carapace width), and preferred males (> 101 mm). These are alternative definitions of maturity that reflect the uncertainty in the reproductive potential of the stock. The observed survey biomass for each, in the terminal survey year and the year preceding it, is:

\Needspace{9\baselineskip}

```{r survey-currencies, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
svy_tab <- data.frame(
  `Maturity definition` = c("Morphometrically mature males", "Large males (>= 95 mm)",
               "Preferred males (> 101 mm)"),
  `2025`   = c(survey_morph_2025, survey_large_2025, survey_pref_2025),
  `2026`   = c(survey_morph_2026, survey_large_2026, survey_pref_2026),
  `Change (%)` = 100 * (c(survey_morph_2026, survey_large_2026, survey_pref_2026) /
                        c(survey_morph_2025, survey_large_2025, survey_pref_2025) - 1),
  check.names = FALSE
)
flextable::flextable(svy_tab) |>
  flextable::colformat_double(digits = 2) |>
  flextable::autofit() |>
  flextable::set_caption(
    caption = paste("Observed NMFS summer survey male biomass (1,000 t) by maturity definition,",
                    "for the terminal survey year and the one preceding it. These are",
                    "survey observations, not output of any assessment model. The Tier 4",
                    "calculation below is applied to the REMA-smoothed series."),
    autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "survey-currencies")
  )
```

The preferred-male estimate is reported in full because it is the measure industry and the State track. The 2026 survey estimates `r .f(pref_abund_2026, 2)` million preferred males (survey CV `r .f(100*pref_abund_cv_2026, 1)` percent), a biomass of `r .f(survey_pref_2026, 2)` kt (CV `r .f(100*pref_biom_cv_2026, 1)` percent). This is a decline of `r .f(abs(pref_biom_chg), 1)` percent in biomass and `r .f(abs(pref_abund_chg), 1)` percent in abundance from 2025, and it leaves preferred-male biomass the `r if (!is.na(pref_rank_2026)) paste0(pref_rank_2026, if (pref_rank_2026 %% 10 == 1 && pref_rank_2026 != 11) 'st' else if (pref_rank_2026 %% 10 == 2 && pref_rank_2026 != 12) 'nd' else if (pref_rank_2026 %% 10 == 3 && pref_rank_2026 != 13) 'rd' else 'th') else 'NA'` lowest in the `r pref_n_yrs`-year series, at `r .f(pref_pct_mean, 0)` percent of its long-term mean. The 2025 value was itself a two-year recovery from the 2023 low, and that recovery has not continued. Morphometrically mature male biomass, which the control rule acts on, is nearly unchanged over the same year (Table \@ref(tab:survey-currencies)), so the choice of maturity definition, rather than the survey, determines whether the stock appears stable or declining.

Applying the Tier 4 rule to each maturity definition gives:

names(t4) <- c("Maturity definition", "B_MSY", "B current", "Status", "M", "F_OFL", "OFL",

<!---BLOCK_LANDSCAPE_STOP--->
\elandscape


Morphometrically mature male biomass is the definition of maturity used, as directed by the SSC (Section B), giving an OFL of `r .f(ofl_2026)` kt and, after the `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100*(1-ABC_buffer))` buffer, an ABC of `r .f(abc_2026)` kt. The authors caution that fishing at the resulting OFL could remove a considerable proportion of industry-preferred males: the OFL of `r .f(ofl_2026, 2)` kt is `r .f(100*ofl_2026/survey_pref_2026, 0)` percent of the observed preferred-male survey biomass (Table \@ref(tab:survey-currencies)). This comparison does not account for natural mortality between the survey and the fishery, nor for the discard mortality entailed in taking that catch.

The guidelines require reporting the uncertainty in the biomass used by the control rule. The REMA model estimates terminal morphometrically mature male biomass at `r .f(mmb_2026, 2)` kt with a 95 percent confidence interval of `r .f(mmb_2026_lci, 2)` to `r .f(mmb_2026_uci, 2)` kt (a coefficient of variation of `r .f(100*mmb_2026_cv, 1)` percent). This is the interval REMA returns for the smoothed series, reflecting the process error the REMA model estimates. It is not the sampling uncertainty of the survey itself: the survey CVs are an input to the fit, not an output. The assumed distribution was lognormal, so the log-scale standard deviation is (log of the upper bound minus log of the lower bound) divided by 2 x 1.96, and the coefficient of variation follows from it.

Propagating that interval through the control rule and the catch equation gives an OFL of `r .f(ofl_2026, 2)` kt with a 95 percent confidence interval of `r .f(ofl_2026_lci, 2)` to `r .f(ofl_2026_uci, 2)` kt. The OFL interval is wider than the biomass interval because F~OFL~ also rises with status under the sloped rule: at the lower bound F~OFL~ falls to `r .f(t4_rec$Fofl_lci, 3)` and at the upper bound it reaches M (`r .f(t4_rec$Fofl_uci, 3)`). Stock status is `r .f(status_2026, 3)` with a 95 percent confidence interval of `r .f(status_2026_lci, 3)` to `r .f(status_2026_uci, 3)`. The lower bound is above the minimum stock size threshold of `r .f(msst_2026, 2)` kt, so the stock is not overfished at any point in the interval. The upper bound exceeds one, so a rebuilt stock cannot be excluded (Section H).

This interval reflects the REMA process error only. It does not include uncertainty in the B~MSY~ proxy, the choice of maturity definition, or the averaging window.

The recommended Tier 4 model involves two choices, the control rule and the catch equation, and each is reported with its alternative so the effect of either can be seen directly.

The control rule is the sloped Tier 4 rule from the crab FMP, under which F~OFL~ ramps linearly from zero at the closure threshold to M at the B~MSY~ proxy: F~OFL~ = M (B/B~MSY~ - alpha) / (1 - alpha), with alpha = 0.10 and a closure threshold beta = 0.25. At the current status of `r .f(status_2026, 3)` this gives F~OFL~ = `r .f(fofl_2026, 4)` compared with M = `r .f(NAT_M, 2)`.

The flat alternative, F~OFL~ = M above the closure threshold with no ramp, is reported for comparison: it raises F~OFL~ to `r .f(fofl_2026_flat, 4)` and the OFL from `r .f(ofl_2026, 2)` to `r .f(ofl_2026_flat, 2)` kt, a difference of `r .f(100*(ofl_2026_flat/ofl_2026 - 1), 0)` percent. It is not recommended. The flat form has sometimes been defended by analogy with the groundfish Tier 5 rule, under which the target rate is the natural mortality rate with no ramp, but that analogy does not apply to this stock: the crab and groundfish FMPs define separate and independent tier systems, and a crab stock assessed under crab Tier 4 takes the crab Tier 4 control rule.

Here we use the Baranov catch equation, changed this cycle from the linear form used previously. F~OFL~ is an instantaneous rate and natural mortality acts on the stock over the same year, so the yield taken by fishing is the fishing component of the total mortality Z = F + M rather than F applied to the starting biomass. The incorrectly applied linear form F~OFL~ x B is the first-order approximation and always biases the OFL high. The bias is large here because F~OFL~ is of the same order as M (at F~OFL~ = M, fishing is exactly half of Z). On this cycle's biomass, holding the rate at F~OFL~ = M so that only the equation changes, the linear form gives `r .f(ofl_2026_linear, 2)` kt compared with `r .f(ofl_2026_flat, 2)` kt from the Baranov. The linear form is retained in Table \@ref(tab:tier4-currencies) because the other BSAI crab Tier 4 assessments use it, which keeps the comparison across stocks. However, the author does not recommend its use given the clear bias.

The basis the SSC used to set the 2025/26 specification can be inferred from its reported values. At a stock status of 0.74 the SSC reported F~OFL~ = 0.19 (October 2025 SSC report, Table 2). A flat F = M rule would have given 0.27, whereas the sloped rule at that status gives M x (0.74 - 0.10) / (1 - 0.10) = 0.192. The specified OFL of 20.11 kt divided by the MMB of 105.213 kt implies F~OFL~ = 0.1911. The 2025/26 specification was therefore set with the sloped rule and the linear catch equation. This assessment applies the same sloped rule, so the control rule is no longer a point of divergence. The remaining difference is the catch equation, which lowers the OFL relative to the linear form the SSC used.


## Parameters estimated independently of the assessment

The Tier 4 model does not estimate biological parameters. The one quantity it takes as given is natural mortality (first bullet below). The remaining quantities listed are fixed inputs to the Tier 3 models:

* **Natural mortality**, M = `r .f(NAT_M, 2)` yr^-1^ for mature males. This is the median of the prior on natural mortality used in the integrated assessment. It is the target fishing mortality at the B~MSY~ proxy and the maximum from which the Tier 4 control rule ramps down below it.
* **The probability of terminal molt at size**, supplied as a fixed input from the Kodiak laboratory's spatiotemporal `sdmTMB` maturity workflow rather than estimated within the model.
* **The variance in the growth increment**, specified rather than estimated. Mean growth per molt is estimated within the assessment, and the model is fit to the growth data (Figure \@ref(fig:growthfits)). Only the variability about the predicted post-molt size is fixed.
* **Weight at length**, specified from the published relationship.
* **Discard and bycatch mortality rates**, specified rather than estimated.

## Status determination

**Is the stock subject to overfishing?** No. Overfishing is determined by comparing the catch from the most recent complete crab year with the OFL specified for that year. Total catch in 2025/26 was 7.10 kt: 4.13 kt retained, 2.52 kt of male and 0.03 kt of female discarded catch from the directed fishery, and 0.42 kt of non-directed bycatch, of which 0.04 kt was taken in the groundfish trawl fisheries and 0.38 kt in other crab fisheries. These are catches, not mortalities: the 30 percent handling mortality on directed discards is applied inside the assessment model rather than to the data. Total catch is compared to the OFL of 20.11 kt that the SSC specified for 2025/26 in October 2025. Catch was 35 percent of the specified OFL.

**Is the stock overfished?** No. The stock was determined to be overfished for 2024/25, with mature male biomass of 60.08 kt against a minimum stock size threshold of 71.40 kt (October 2025 SSC report, Table 1), and it remains in the rebuilding plan adopted under Amendment 53. On this cycle's estimate mature male biomass is `r .f(mmb_2026, 2)` kt against a minimum stock size threshold of `r .f(msst_2026, 2)` kt, so the stock is above the threshold on the current estimate and across the whole of its 95 percent confidence interval (Section F).

**Is the stock approaching an overfished condition?** Unknown. Answering this question requires a reliable projection of mature male biomass. The Tier 3 models do not converge reliably and their recruitment estimates have high retrospective bias, and the Tier 4 assessment produces no projection, so no reliable projection is available.

\newpage

## F~limit~

Under the Tier 4 control rule, the fishing mortality rate above which the stock is considered subject to overfishing is the natural mortality rate when biomass is at or above the B~MSY~ proxy. Under the FMP ramp it is reduced below that point. This document applies the FMP ramp (Section F), so at the current status of `r .f(status_2026, 3)` the F~limit~ is `r .f(fofl_2026, 3)` yr^-1^ rather than M. Under the flat alternative it would be M = `r .f(NAT_M, 2)` yr^-1^ across the whole range above the closure threshold. This is a different quantity from the reverse-engineered F reported for Tier 1-3 stocks, which is the rate that would have produced a catch equal to the previous year's OFL. That quantity is not computed here.

\newpage

# G. Calculation of the ABC

The recommended acceptable biological catch (ABC) is calculated by subtracting a buffer from the OFL to account for scientific uncertainty. The buffer applied here is `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*(1-ABC_buffer))` percent, giving an ABC of `r .f(abc_2026, 2)` kt against an OFL of `r .f(ofl_2026, 2)` kt.

The buffer accounts for the considerable scientific uncertainty in the Tier 4 OFL: the 95 percent confidence interval on the OFL ranges from `r .f(ofl_2026_lci, 2)` to `r .f(ofl_2026_uci, 2)` kt, and the choice of maturity definition changes the OFL by more than that interval (Section F). A larger buffer was not considered necessary for two reasons. The ESP indicates favorable conditions for juvenile snow crab (Table \@ref(tab:risk-table)), and the Tier 4 OFL of `r .f(ofl_2026, 2)` kt is considerably lower than the Tier 3 OFLs, which range from 43.8 to 147.3 kt across the models presented (Table \@ref(tab:stepchange)).

The June 2026 SSC supported reporting a stock-specific history of the buffers applied to the OFL, and supported the CPT's suggestion that a historical buffer could initially be set at the average buffer from the previous five assessments (Table \@ref(tab:buffer-history)).

```{r buffer-history, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F}
# Five years, 2021-2025: the checklist asks for a five-year buffer history and
# the June 2026 SSC proposes "the average buffer from the previous five
# assessments". 2021 as printed in the 2025 SAFE; 2022-2025 from Table 2 of each
# October SSC report -- the 2022 report was thought unavailable and its 25% was
# NA until it was located (2026-08-29).
buffer_hist <- data.frame(
  Year   = c(2021L, 2022L, 2023L, 2024L, 2025L),
  Buffer = c(25, 25, 50, 65, 40),
  Source = c("2025 SAFE, Section G",
             "October 2022 SSC report, Table 2",
             "October 2023 SSC report, Table 2",
             "October 2024 SSC report, Table 2",
             "October 2025 SSC report, Table 2"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
.known <- buffer_hist$Buffer[!is.na(buffer_hist$Buffer)]
buffer_hist$Buffer <- ifelse(is.na(buffer_hist$Buffer), "NA",
                             sprintf("%.0f%%", buffer_hist$Buffer))
names(buffer_hist)[2] <- "SSC buffer (% of OFL)"

flextable::flextable(buffer_hist) |>
  # Crab years, not measurements: flextable's default integer formatting applies
  # big.mark and printed them "2,020" (fixed 2026-08-29).
  flextable::colformat_int(j = "Year", big.mark = "") |>
  flextable::autofit() |>
  flextable::set_caption(
    caption = sprintf(paste("History of the ABC buffer applied by the SSC, as a percentage of the",
                            "OFL, for the %d most recent assessments. The mean is %.0f%%.",
                            "Each value is read from Table 2 of the October SSC report for that",
                            "year, except 2021, which is as printed in the September",
                            "2025 assessment."),
                      length(.known), mean(.known)),
    autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "buffer-history")
  )
```

The `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*(1-ABC_buffer))` percent buffer matches the September 2025 assessment's recommendation and is the buffer historically applied to crab stocks with data and model complexity sufficient for Tier 3. It is lower than the buffers the SSC has applied to this stock in recent years. For the 2025/26 specification the SSC applied a 40 percent buffer, setting an ABC of 12.07 kt against an OFL of 20.11 kt (October 2025 SSC report, Table 2). Against the history in Table \@ref(tab:buffer-history), a 20 percent buffer would be the smallest applied to this stock in any of the five years shown and about half the `r sprintf("%.0f", mean(.known))` percent average.

The recommended OFL of `r .f(ofl_2026, 2)` kt is `r if (mp_have) sprintf("%.0f", abs(100*(ofl_2026/mp$ofl[mp$crab_year == "2025/26"] - 1))) else "NA"` percent below the `r if (mp_have) .f(mp$ofl[mp$crab_year == "2025/26"], 2) else "NA"` kt specified for 2025/26, yet the recommended ABC of `r .f(abc_2026, 2)` kt is `r if (mp_have) sprintf("%.0f", 100*(abc_2026/mp$abc[mp$crab_year == "2025/26"] - 1)) else "NA"` percent above the `r if (mp_have) .f(mp$abc[mp$crab_year == "2025/26"], 2) else "NA"` kt specified, given the change in buffer from 40 percent to 20 percent. The biomass the control rule acts on is nearly unchanged: the smoothed mature-male series rose about 4 percent, and the survey observation behind it fell about 3 percent (Figure \@ref(fig:rema-fit)). The rise in the ABC is therefore entirely a consequence of the buffer, not of a change in the stock or the control rule. The contrast is sharper against the measure industry tracks: preferred-male biomass fell `r .f(abs(pref_biom_chg), 1)` percent over the same year, to the `r if (!is.na(pref_rank_2026)) paste0(pref_rank_2026, if (pref_rank_2026 %% 10 == 1 && pref_rank_2026 != 11) 'st' else if (pref_rank_2026 %% 10 == 2 && pref_rank_2026 != 12) 'nd' else if (pref_rank_2026 %% 10 == 3 && pref_rank_2026 != 13) 'rd' else 'th') else 'NA'` lowest value in `r pref_n_yrs` years (Table \@ref(tab:survey-currencies)). With the control rule no longer in dispute, the difference between this recommendation and the 2025/26 specification rests on the buffer and on the choice of maturity definition discussed in Section F rather than on any change in stock trend. In the current-year row, the assessment-related, ecosystem and fishery-informed categories score Level 1, Normal, and the population dynamics category scores Level 2, Increased concern, reflecting the low observed biomass of industry-preferred males (Table \@ref(tab:risk-table)).

\newpage

## Risk table

The risk table follows the four categories used for groundfish, in the tiered form the June 2026 SSC described: a long-term row for persistent uncertainty, which is what justifies a base or historical buffer, and a current-year row for year-specific risk. The SSC scopes the long-term row to the assessment and population-dynamics categories only, so the ecosystem and fishery cells in that row are not scored.

The ecosystem and fishery-informed cells below are taken from the 2026 risk table summary prepared from the ESP (Fedewa and Shotwell 2026), the AFSC Spring Preview of Ecosystem and Economic Conditions Workshop, and the eastern Bering Sea Ecosystem Status Report (Siddon 2026, in press). The risk table summary scores current-year population dynamics Level 1, Normal. The authors raise that cell to Level 2, Increased concern, because the observed biomass of industry-preferred males is the fourth lowest in the 44-year survey time series. The ESP is Appendix A to this assessment.

```{r risk-table, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F}
# Grid transcribed from 'Snow Crab ESP-ESR Risk Table Summary 2026.docx' and
# updated 2026-09-08 from the revised summary ('... 2026 (2).docx'). The
# assessment-related cells and the long-term population dynamics cell were left
# for the author there; levels assigned by GA review 2026-08-31.
risk_tab <- data.frame(
  Category = c("Assessment-related", "Population dynamics",
               "Ecosystem", "Fishery-informed stock"),
  `Long-term / persistent` = c(
    paste("Level 2: Increased concern. Multimodality has persisted across assessment cycles and is",
          "the reason the stock moved from Tier 3 to Tier 4. Jittering the accepted model returns to",
          "the reported fit in only 1.3 percent of converged runs.",
          "A likelihood improvement of 1.27 units moved the OFL",
          "of Model 26.1 by 12.8 percent. Successive assessments have revised the same historical",
          "years by up to an order of magnitude (Section E, Historical analysis), which is far larger",
          "than the within-model retrospective pattern. The base model estimates on the order of four",
          "hundred parameters, many highly correlated, which the June 2026 SSC identified as",
          "consistent with overparameterization."),
    paste("Level 2: Increased concern. There is considerable uncertainty regarding the population",
          "dynamics estimated in the GMACS model. Estimates of M across the various models have",
          "large CVs and recruitment estimates have been shown to have high retrospective bias.",
          "There is also evidence of decreasing size-at-maturity and an increasing proportion of",
          "hybrids in the data."),
    "Not scored (long-term row is scoped to the first two categories)",
    "Not scored (long-term row is scoped to the first two categories)"),
  `Current year` = c(
    paste("Level 1: Normal. The OFL is based on a Tier 4 assessment whose terminal biomass has a CV",
          "of 14.8 percent, a 95 percent confidence interval of 85.4 to 152.1 kt, and a status",
          "interval of 0.58 to 1.04 that spans the rebuilt threshold."),
    paste("Level 2: Increased concern. Observed biomass of industry-preferred males (> 101 mm) is",
          "the fourth lowest in the 44-year survey time series. A highly female-skewed sex ratio,",

    paste("Level 1: Normal. Spring 2026 offshelf transport moved crab away from suitable benthic",

          "concerns are minor with uncertain impacts on the stock."),
    paste("Level 1: Normal. Fishery-informed indicators generally support stable stock condition.",
          "Shifts in fleet behavior appear motivated primarily by weather, sorting, fuel costs and",

  check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

## Author recommendations

The June 2026 SSC recommended that only the Tier 4 model be brought forward in October, to allow time for the development of a simpler and more stable Tier 3 model. The overfishing limit is calculated on that basis. The Tier 3 models are presented to document progress and are not proposed for specification.

Three questions the May 2026 preliminary assessment put to the CPT and SSC have since been settled and are not reopened here. The composition correction and the expanded plus group were endorsed as technical corrections and are included in every September model. The immature survey index was rejected as a convergence fix on the grounds that it shifts the model toward higher natural mortality among mature males and raises a question of duplicative use of the same survey data. Hybrid catch data were judged premature for inclusion in the snow and Tanner crab assessment models, with hybrid-related uncertainty to be handled through the existing ABC buffer-setting process.

The definition of maturity used for management has a large impact on the management recommendations, and given the decreasing size-at-maturity and the potential for density-dependent maturity, the decision opens up uncertainties. The definition also changes the OFL: morphometric maturity gives `r .f(ofl_2026, 2)` kt against `r .f(tier4_by_currency$OFL[tier4_by_currency$currency == ">95 mm"], 2)` kt on >= 95 mm and `r .f(tier4_by_currency$OFL[tier4_by_currency$currency == ">101 mm"], 2)` kt on > 101 mm (Table \@ref(tab:tier4-currencies)). The 2025 assessment recommended >= 95 mm, arguing that morphometric reference points permit the removal of essentially all large males while the trend in large males is firmly negative.

The author's priorities for the coming cycle are to identify and construct a simplified Tier 3 model (fixing the recruitment sex ratio at 50:50, reducing confounding among growth, natural mortality and selectivity, estimating growth externally, and considering an earlier equilibrium start year) in preference to further iterations of the current base model. The male-only model (`Model 26.2`) is a first step in that direction and is reported here. Additionally, improvements to data treatment following discussions with the CPT are a priority, particularly the construction of separate immature and mature data sets.

A yield-per-recruit analysis, requested by the SSC in June 2025 and again in June 2026 to inform development of an alternative harvest control rule, has not been completed for this cycle and is a priority for the next cycle, in addition to an MSE to identify improved harvest control rules.

# H. Rebuilding analysis and update

## Status of the rebuilding plan

On 19 October 2021 NMFS determined, and notified the Council, that the eastern Bering Sea snow crab stock was overfished, the estimated mature male biomass having fallen below the minimum stock size threshold specified in the fishery management plan. The Council developed a rebuilding plan under section 304(e) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act, adopted as Amendment 53 to the Fishery Management Plan for Bering Sea/Aleutian Islands King and Tanner Crabs and implemented before the start of the 2023/24 fishing season.

The rebuilding analysis set the minimum time to rebuild in the absence of fishing (T~min~) at 6 years, which under the National Standard 1 guidelines sets a maximum time to rebuild (T~max~) of 10 years. The stock is considered rebuilt when mature male biomass reaches B~MSY~. Median projections placed rebuilding in 2029 under no fishing, under bycatch only, and under the State harvest strategy, and in 2030 under fishing at the ABC. The 5th inter-simulation percentile is 2027 across all scenarios. The 95th is 2034 under no fishing and under bycatch only. Under the State harvest strategy and under fishing at the ABC the upper tail does not rebuild within the projection horizon. If mortality events of the kind observed in 2018-19 recur in roughly one year in seven, the projected rebuilding time under no fishing extends to 2034, and under the State harvest strategy and under fishing at the ABC the stock does not rebuild within the projection horizon. The analysis concluded that the main driver of the rate of rebuilding is recruitment and the ecosystem conditions that permit it, rather than fishing mortality.

## Relationship to previous rebuilding plans

This is the third rebuilding plan for the stock. Snow crab was first declared overfished on 24 September 1999, and a rebuilding plan was adopted as Amendment 14 in 2000. The Amendment 53 environmental assessment's reference list cites Amendment 15 for that plan, but the 2000 environmental assessment itself is titled for Amendment 14 (NPFMC, ADF&G and NMFS staff, December 2000), and Amendment 14 is cited here. In 2009 the NMFS Alaska Region notified the Council that the stock would not be rebuilt by the end of that rebuilding period, 2009/10, and that a revised plan was required. Amendment 39 followed. Amendment 53 replaces those earlier provisions, which were removed from the fishery management plan when it was adopted.

## Progress toward rebuilding

Mature male biomass is estimated at `r .f(mmb_2026, 2)` kt against a B~MSY~ proxy of `r .f(bmsy_2026, 2)` kt, or `r .f(100*status_2026, 0)` percent of the proxy, with a minimum stock size threshold of `r .f(msst_2026, 2)` kt. The stock is above its minimum stock size threshold but has not, on the point estimate, reached the biomass at which it would be considered rebuilt. Accounting for the uncertainty in the random-effects fit (Section F), status is `r .f(status_2026, 3)` with a 95 percent confidence interval of `r .f(status_2026_lci, 3)` to `r .f(status_2026_uci, 3)`. The lower end remains above the threshold for an overfished determination and the upper end reaches the rebuilt threshold, so the stock cannot be declared rebuilt, but rebuilding cannot be excluded on the terminal-year estimate alone.

## Recruitment

Because the rebuilding analysis identifies recruitment as the main driver of the rebuilding rate, recruitment is reported here directly. Estimated male recruitment from the author-preferred Tier 3 model (`Model 26.1b`) collapsed to 0.088 and 0.065 billion crab in 2018 and 2019, among the lowest in the time series, before rising to 1.65, 2.36 and 4.28 billion in 2020, 2021 and 2022 and settling near 1.0 billion in 2024 and 2025. The mean over the last five years, 2.01 billion, is above the 1982 to 2019 mean of 1.22 billion.

That comparison should be treated with caution. Terminal-year recruitment is the least well determined quantity in the assessment: the retrospective analysis gives a Mohn's rho for male recruitment of `r .fmt(.rho("standard","recruitment_male"), 2)`, meaning that recent recruitment estimates change substantially as data accumulate. The apparent post-collapse recruitment pulse is consistent with the survey observing small crab, but its magnitude in the terminal years should not be relied on. Terminal recruitment is not used in the reference-point calculations, and recruits are observed in the survey for roughly five years before entering the fishery, so the practical consequence of this uncertainty for management is limited.

\newpage

# I. Data gaps and research priorities

Several data and structural issues warrant follow-up:

* **Hybrid identification consistency between ADF&G and NMFS.** ADF&G classifies hybrid crab into three categories (opilio-type, bairdi-type, and unspecified) using a hybrid identification key based on eye color, epistome shape, and secondary morphological characteristics. ADF&G and NMFS do not currently agree on the number of secondary characteristics required for a positive hybrid identification, and the unspecified-hybrid category is present in a non-trivial portion of the time series. Resolving identification criteria across agencies and propagating the resulting categorization back through the historical observer time series would improve the hybrid-data products available to the assessment. However, the benefit to the snow crab assessment may be minimal given the low percentage of opilio-type hybrids in the data.

* **Apportionment of retained catch between snow crab and hybrids.** Hybrids are currently retained under either the snow-crab or the Tanner-crab IFQ depending on regulatory identification but are not separately tracked in the retained-catch data. ADF&G has indicated it does not yet have a method for partitioning historical retained catch into hybrid versus parent species. Developing such a partitioning would allow the hybrid sensitivity to be explored more fully (presently the retained time series is identical between the hybrid and non-hybrid configurations evaluated in May 2026 because retained catch already contains hybrids).

* **Quality control on early hybrid catch estimates.** The ADF&G hybrid total-catch estimates contain unexpectedly large values in 1997 (~18 kt of legal-male hybrid catch) and 1998 (~15 kt), with high-CPUE pots peppered around the fishery footprint rather than concentrated in obvious hot spots. ADF&G has flagged these years as requiring follow-up before the data should be considered reliable for regular assessment use.

* **Maturity workflow comparison.** The new spatiotemporal maturity workflow produces a much weaker temporal trend in the probability of terminal molt at size than the legacy workflow. Side-by-side documentation of the two workflows, an evaluation of the spatial sample sizes of chela measurements (which are sparse at many stations and many sizes), uncertainty, and quantification of the degrees of freedom consumed by the spatial process would help the CPT and SSC evaluate the two approaches.

* **Source of the multiple minima in the snow crab assessment.** The immature survey index removed the bimodal jitter signal seen in the May 2026 candidate models, but the underlying source of the multiple minima (six in the author-preferred model this cycle) is not understood. The jitter attribution in Section E identifies the parameters that most separate the six minima, but not why those combinations are alternative solutions. Extending that work to the correlation structure and to likelihood profiles would clarify whether the immature index solves a real problem or masks it.

* **Reproductive biology of large male snow crab.** As noted in 2024 and 2025 SSC comments, more research is needed on whether small males can and do mate with large females and produce progeny that will be large males under favorable environmental conditions, and on what determines terminal molt. This question remains the main axis of uncertainty because the fishery cannot exist without large males and large males are at historical lows.

```{r survey-series, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
## The observed survey series the Tier 4 calculation is built on. Design-based
## NMFS summer trawl survey estimates -- no assessment model is involved. Shown
## in full because the Tier 4 recommendation rests on this series and the
## document otherwise gives it only for the terminal two years (Table
## \@ref(tab:survey-currencies)) and as points on Figure \@ref(fig:rema-fit).
## Requested by a PSC-limit user who needed a model-free survey number, 2026-09.
.mm <- read.csv("data/derived/survey_indices.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
.mm <- .mm[.mm$sex == "male" & .mm$maturity == "mature", c("year", "biomass", "cv")]
.lg <- read.csv("data/survey/survey_large_male_index_derived.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
.cat <- function(k) {
  d <- .lg[.lg$CATEGORY == k, c("YEAR", "BIOMASS_MT", "BIOMASS_MT_CV")]
  names(d) <- c("year", "biomass", "cv")
  d$biomass <- d$biomass / 1000      # t -> 1,000 t, the document's units
  d
}
.fmtbc <- function(b, cv) ifelse(is.na(b), "--", sprintf("%.1f (%.2f)", b, cv))
svy_series <- Reduce(function(a, b) merge(a, b, by = "year", all = TRUE),
  list(setNames(.mm,             c("year", "b_mm", "cv_mm")),
       setNames(.cat("large_male"),    c("year", "b_95", "cv_95")),
       setNames(.cat("preferred_male"), c("year", "b_101", "cv_101"))))
svy_series <- svy_series[order(svy_series$year), ]
stopifnot("survey series must not contain a 2020 row (survey cancelled)" =
            !(2020 %in% svy_series$year))
## Total survey abundance, the quantity the PSC limit is set from. 50 CFR
## 679.21(e)(1)(iii) sets the C. opilio limit from "total abundance of C. opilio
## as indicated by the NMFS annual bottom trawl survey", so this column is the
## DESIGN-BASED survey estimate and includes crab < 25 mm.
##
## The model's own total is deliberately NOT shown here (Grant, 2026-09). It is
## not subject to survey selectivity and runs a median 2.1x the survey estimate,
## so putting the two side by side invites the wrong one being used to set the
## limit. The model total remains available on its own in Table
## \@ref(tab:predtotnum).
.ta <- read.csv("data/derived/survey_total_abundance.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
svy_series <- merge(svy_series, .ta[, c("year", "abundance")], by = "year", all.x = TRUE)
## any() would pass on a single joined year; a key-type drift leaving 43 of 44
## rows as "--" would sail through. Require every survey year to carry a total.
stopifnot("total survey abundance failed to join onto the survey series" =
            !anyNA(svy_series$abundance))

svy_tab_full <- data.frame(
  Year                          = as.integer(svy_series$year),
  `Morphometrically mature`     = .fmtbc(svy_series$b_mm,  svy_series$cv_mm),
  `Males >= 95 mm`              = .fmtbc(svy_series$b_95,  svy_series$cv_95),
  `Males > 101 mm`              = .fmtbc(svy_series$b_101, svy_series$cv_101),
  `Total abundance`             = ifelse(is.na(svy_series$abundance), "--",
                                         sprintf("%.1f", svy_series$abundance)),
  check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

flextable::flextable(svy_tab_full) |>
  flextable::set_table_properties(opts_pdf = list(caption_repeat = FALSE)) |>
  flextable::colformat_int(j = "Year", big.mark = "") |>
  flextable::fontsize(size = 8, part = "all") |>
  flextable::align(j = 2:5, align = "right", part = "all") |>
  ## Same page-width guard as the other wide tables: autofit sizes columns from
  ## content, fit_to_width rescales to the 6.5 in portrait line (2026-09-09).
  flextable::autofit() |>
  flextable::fit_to_width(max_width = 6.4) |>
  flextable::set_caption(
    caption = paste(
      "Survey biomass and total abundance, from the NMFS summer bottom trawl survey. All values are",
      "design-based survey estimates; no assessment model is involved. Columns 2-4 are male biomass",
      "(1,000 t) by maturity definition, coefficient of variation in parentheses, and are the series",
      "the random-effects (REMA) model of Section F is fit to; the morphometric CV is the legal-male",
      "(>= 78 mm) value, used as a proxy. Column 5 is total abundance (millions of crab, both",
      "sexes, all maturity stages, including crab < 25 mm), the quantity 50 CFR 679.21(e)(1)(iii)",
      "specifies for the C. opilio prohibited species catch limit. No survey in 2020."),
    autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "survey-series"))
```

```{r rema-series, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
## The smoothed series the Tier 4 reference points are computed from. The
## terminal value is the biomass the control rule acts on; the mean over the
## whole series is the B_MSY proxy. 2020 HAS a row here and not in the observed
## table above -- that is the point of the random-effects fit.
.rp <- read.csv("data/tier4/rema_predictions.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
.pick <- function(k) {
  d <- .rp[.rp$size == k, c("Year", "rema_pred", "rema_lci", "rema_uci")]
  d <- d[order(d$Year), ]
  data.frame(Year = d$Year,
             v = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f-%.1f)", d$rema_pred, d$rema_lci, d$rema_uci),
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
rema_tab <- Reduce(function(a, b) merge(a, b, by = "Year", all = TRUE),
  list(setNames(.pick("morphometric"), c("Year", "Morphometrically mature")),
       setNames(.pick("95"),           c("Year", "Males >= 95 mm")),
       setNames(.pick("101"),          c("Year", "Males > 101 mm"))))
rema_tab$Year <- as.integer(rema_tab$Year)
stopifnot("REMA series should carry 2020, which the survey does not" =
            2020 %in% rema_tab$Year)

flextable::flextable(rema_tab) |>
  flextable::set_table_properties(opts_pdf = list(caption_repeat = FALSE)) |>
  flextable::colformat_int(j = "Year", big.mark = "") |>
  flextable::fontsize(size = 8, part = "all") |>
  flextable::align(j = 2:4, align = "right", part = "all") |>
  flextable::autofit() |>
  flextable::fit_to_width(max_width = 6.4) |>
  flextable::set_caption(
    caption = paste(
      "Random-effects (REMA) smoothed survey biomass (1,000 t), 95 percent prediction interval in",
      "parentheses, by maturity definition. The terminal year is the biomass the Tier 4 control rule",
      "acts on; the mean over the series is the BMSY proxy. 2020 has a fitted value although the",
      "survey was cancelled, which is why the proxy averages the smoothed series, not the",
      "observations."),
    autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "rema-series"))
```

# All three columns are keyed off the SAME names, so no positional list can
# drift out of step (model_jittered lives in 0-models.R beside the definitions).
# models_present, not model_defs, so a model that has not been built yet is
# absent from the table rather than present as a blank row.
# NO `Updates` column. It held names(models_present) -- the INTERNAL case keys
# ("26.1 gmacs (update + compfix + plus group + new_mat + male_only)"), which
# 0-models.R states must never reach a table or figure. Printing them put the
# join keys in front of the CPT and made this table 16 in wide, the single
# worst overfull box in the document. `Purpose` already says what each model
# changes (fixed 2026-08-29).
model_overview = data.frame(
  Model    = unname(model_shorts[names(models_present)]),
  Type     = unname(model_type[names(models_present)]),
  Jittered = c(Y = "Yes", n = "No")[unname(model_jittered[names(models_present)])],
  Purpose  = unname(model_purpose[names(models_present)]),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
model_overview <- model_overview[order(to_short(names(models_present))), ]
stopifnot("model-overview: Jittered failed to map to Yes/No" =
            !anyNA(model_overview$Jittered))

flextable::flextable(model_overview) |>
  flextable::fontsize(size = 9, part = "all") |>
  # Purpose is a sentence, so give it an explicit width and let it wrap rather
  # than letting autofit() set the table's width from the longest sentence.
  flextable::width(j = c("Model", "Type", "Jittered"), width = c(0.95, 0.85, 0.75)) |>
  flextable::width(j = "Purpose", width = 3.7) |>
  flextable::set_caption(
    caption = "Overview of the models presented in the September 2026 assessment, with the type and purpose of each. 'Jittered' records whether a jitter analysis was run for that model this cycle. The same four models received retrospective sweeps (Table \\@ref(tab:retro-rho)).",
    autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "model-overview")
  )

```{r like-index-tot, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F}

extract_likelihoods <- function(path) {
  out_file <- file.path(path, "Gmacsall.out")
  if (!file.exists(out_file)) return(NULL)

  tmp <- readLines(out_file)

  # Pull the Raw_likelihood vector for a labeled sub-block of
  # Likelihoods_by_type_and_fleet (e.g. "Catches", "Index", "Size_composition").
  get_raw <- function(label) {
    hdr <- grep(paste0("^--", label, ": list"), tmp)[1]
    if (is.na(hdr)) return(numeric(0))
    eol_offset <- grep("^>EOL<", tmp[(hdr + 1):length(tmp)])[1]
    block <- tmp[(hdr + 1):(hdr + eol_offset - 1)]
    raw <- block[grep("^Raw_likelihood", block)][1]
    parts <- strsplit(trimws(sub("^Raw_likelihood\\s*:?\\s*", "", raw)), "\\s+")[[1]]
    as.numeric(parts)
  }

  ## Component labels are DERIVED FROM EACH MODEL, not assumed.
  ##
  ## These were fixed vectors of length 4/4/13, applied positionally. GMACS
  ## emits one likelihood per component the model actually has, so the male-only
  ## model -- which has 3 catch, 2 index and 7 size components -- had every value
  ## after the first divergence shifted onto the wrong label, and the table
  ## showed a model with no female population fitting four female components
  ## while its male survey data read as 0.00 (found 2026-08-29).
  ##
  ## The fit summaries carry fleet, sex, type and maturity per series, in the
  ## same order as the likelihood vectors, so build the labels from them. For the
  ## two-sex models this reproduces the previous vectors exactly.
  .block <- function(header, keys) {
    st <- grep(paste0("^", header, ": dataframe"), tmp)[1]
    if (is.na(st)) return(character(0))
    hdr <- strsplit(trimws(tmp[st + 1]), " +")[[1]]
    rows <- character(0)
    for (ln in tmp[(st + 2):length(tmp)]) {
      if (!nzchar(trimws(ln)) || startsWith(ln, ">")) break
      rows <- c(rows, ln)
    }
    if (!length(rows)) return(character(0))
    m <- do.call(rbind, lapply(strsplit(trimws(rows), " +"), function(x) {
      length(x) <- length(hdr); x
    }))
    colnames(m) <- hdr
    if (!all(keys %in% hdr)) return(character(0))
    sig <- apply(m[, keys, drop = FALSE], 1, paste, collapse = "\u001f")
    unique(sig)
  }
  .fleet <- function(x) c(Pot_Fishery = "Pot", Trawl_Bycatch = "Trawl",
                          NMFS_Trawl_1982 = "NMFS 1982",
                          NMFS_Trawl_1989 = "NMFS 1989")[x]
  .sex   <- function(x) c(male = "M", Male = "M", female = "F", Female = "F",
                          Both = "", both = "")[x]

  catch_lbls <- vapply(strsplit(.block("Catch_fit_summary", c("Fleet","Sex","Type")), "\u001f"),
    function(v) {
      if (v[1] == "Trawl_Bycatch") "Catch: Trawl bycatch"
      else sprintf("Catch: %s %s %s", .fleet(v[1]), tolower(v[3]), .sex(v[2]))
    }, character(1))
  index_lbls <- vapply(strsplit(.block("Index_fit_summary", c("Fleet","Sex","Maturity")), "\u001f"),
    function(v) sprintf("Index: %s %s %s", .fleet(v[1]), .sex(v[2]), tolower(v[3])),
    character(1))
  size_lbls <- vapply(strsplit(.block("Size_fit_summary", c("Fleet","Sex","Type","Maturity")), "\u001f"),
    function(v) {
      if (grepl("^NMFS", v[1])) sprintf("Size: %s %s %s", .fleet(v[1]), .sex(v[2]), tolower(v[4]))
      else sprintf("Size: %s %s %s", .fleet(v[1]), .sex(v[2]), tolower(v[3]))
    }, character(1))

  catch_vals <- get_raw("Catches")
  index_vals <- get_raw("Index")
  size_vals  <- get_raw("Size_composition")

  ## If these ever disagree the labels are wrong, which is exactly the failure
  ## this replaced. Fail the knit rather than print a mislabelled table.
  stopifnot(
    "catch likelihoods do not match the catch fit summary" = length(catch_vals) == length(catch_lbls),
    "index likelihoods do not match the index fit summary" = length(index_vals) == length(index_lbls),
    "size likelihoods do not match the size fit summary"   = length(size_vals)  == length(size_lbls))

  # Other components (SRR, Tag, Growth, Penalties, Priors, ...) still come from
  # the aggregate Likelihoods_by_type block.
  st  <- grep("^Likelihoods_by_type: list", tmp)[1]
  eol_offset <- grep("^>EOL<", tmp[(st + 1):length(tmp)])[1]
  rows <- tmp[(st + 1):(st + eol_offset - 1)]
  clean_rows <- gsub(":", "", rows)
  parts <- strsplit(trimws(clean_rows), " +")
  vals <- sapply(parts, function(x) as.numeric(tail(x, 1)))
  names(vals) <- sapply(parts, function(x) x[1])

  other_keys <- c("Stock_recruitment", "Tagging_data", "Growth_data",
                  "Penalties", "Priors", "Positive_growth_penalty",
                  "Total", "Initial_size_structure")
  other_lbls <- c("SRR", "Tag", "Growth", "Penalties", "Priors",
                  "Positive_growth_penalty", "Total", "Initial_size_structure")
  other_vals <- unname(vals[other_keys])

  dat <- data.frame(
    Object = c(catch_lbls, index_lbls, size_lbls, other_lbls),
    Value  = c(catch_vals, index_vals, size_vals, other_vals)
  )
  colnames(dat)[2] <- path
  return(dat)
}

# models_present, not model_defs: a model that has not been built is absent
# from the table rather than present as a blank column.
tot_likes <- lapply(models_present, extract_likelihoods)

# extract_likelihoods() returns NULL when a model directory has no Gmacsall.out
# -- a fit that never finished writing, not a missing folder, so the dir.exists()
# guard above does not catch it. Left to purrr::reduce() that surfaces as
# `auto_copy(): x and y must share the same src ... y is NULL`, which names
# neither the chunk's real problem nor the model. Name it instead. Hit
# 2026-08-28: Model 26.1a had a complete fit but no Gmacsall.out, and it killed
# the whole render at chunk 18 of 93.
.bad <- names(models_present)[vapply(tot_likes, is.null, logical(1))]
if (length(.bad))
  stop("No Gmacsall.out for: ", paste(to_short(.bad), collapse = ", "),
       ". Re-fit the model, or run gmacs -binp gmacs.bar -hess_step 5 in its ",
       "directory to regenerate the outputs from the existing MLE.")

tot_likes <- tot_likes %>% purrr::reduce(dplyr::full_join)

# NA here means the model HAS NO SUCH COMPONENT (the male-only model has no
# female data), which is not the same as a component that was fitted and
# contributed zero. Filling with 0 conflated the two. Left as NA and rendered as
# a dash by the three table chunks below (2026-08-29).
rownames(tot_likes) <- tot_likes$Object
tot_likes <- tot_likes[,-1]
colnames(tot_likes) <- as.character(to_short(names(models_present)))
# Columns in model-number order, not folder order. models_present follows the
# directory listing, which since the 26.x renumbering puts the male-only model
# (26.2) ahead of the 2019 diagnostic (26.1c). model_order is defined once in
# 0-models.R and is what to_short() already uses for factor levels.
tot_likes <- tot_likes[, intersect(model_order, colnames(tot_likes)), drop = FALSE]

# Render with flextable so the caption produces a Word bookmark/sequence
# field that bookdown's \@ref(tab:like-comp-tot) can resolve. Transposed so
# that models are rows and likelihood components are columns to better fit
# the landscape page.
tot_likes_t <- as.data.frame(t(signif(tot_likes, 5)), check.names = FALSE)
tot_likes_df <- data.frame(
  Model       = rownames(tot_likes_t),
  tot_likes_t,
  check.names = FALSE
)

# Diagnostic dump of the likelihood components, one file per knit date. Nothing
# reads it back -- it exists so the components can be diffed between renders.
# Written to data/diagnostics/, not the repo root: the root is off limits, and
# data/derived/ is the six-file model interface, which this is not part of.
dir.create("data/diagnostics", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
write.csv(tot_likes_t,
          file = file.path("data/diagnostics",
                           paste0("likelihood_components_", Sys.Date(), ".csv")))

# Components in ROWS, models in COLUMNS -- see the note in the composition
# chunk. Six models is a comfortable number of columns; eight long component
# names is not. The "Catch: "/"Index: " prefixes are the slicing keys and are
# kept in the row labels, where there is room for them.
.keep <- grepl("^(Catch|Index): ", rownames(tot_likes))
index_and_catch <- tot_likes[.keep, , drop = FALSE]
index_and_catch <- as.data.frame(lapply(index_and_catch, round, 2),
                                 check.names = FALSE)
index_and_catch <- cbind(
  data.frame(Component = rownames(tot_likes)[.keep], check.names = FALSE),
  index_and_catch)
rownames(index_and_catch) <- NULL

flextable::flextable(index_and_catch) |>
  # A dash marks a component the model does not have (see the NA note above);
  # it is not a fitted value of zero.
  flextable::colformat_double(na_str = "\u2013") |>
  # fontsize BEFORE autofit: autofit() measures the text at the CURRENT size, so
  # shrinking the font afterwards leaves the old, wider column widths in place.
  # set_table_properties(width=) does NOT constrain width in flextable 0.10.0 --
  # measured, it left these tables 13-22 in wide (2026-08-29).
  flextable::fontsize(size = 7, part = "all") |>
  flextable::autofit() |>
  flextable::set_caption(
    caption = "Catch and index likelihood components (negative log-likelihood, dimensionless), one row per component and one column per model. Row labels name the fleet and, where it applies, the sex: M is male, F is female. The two survey rows are the 1982-1988 and 1989-present selectivity eras.",
    autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "like-index-tot")
  )


```

# Components in ROWS, models in COLUMNS -- the opposite of the other two
# likelihood tables. There are thirteen size-composition components and only six
# models, so models-as-rows put thirteen long headers across the page and the
# table measured 22 in wide. tot_likes is already component-by-model.
comp_like <- tot_likes[grepl("^Size: ", rownames(tot_likes)), , drop = FALSE]
comp_like <- as.data.frame(lapply(comp_like, function(x) signif(x, 4)),
                           check.names = FALSE)
rownames(comp_like) <- sub("^Size: ", "", rownames(tot_likes)[grepl("^Size: ", rownames(tot_likes))])

                   comp_like)

Row labels name the fleet, the survey era where it applies (NMFS 1982 is 1982-1988 and NMFS 1989 is 1989-present), the sex (M male, F female) and the maturity state.",

```{r like-other-tot, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F}
# Components in ROWS, models in COLUMNS, as in the other two likelihood tables.
.keep <- !grepl("^(Size|Catch|Index): ", rownames(tot_likes))
other_like <- tot_likes[.keep, , drop = FALSE]
other_like <- as.data.frame(lapply(other_like, function(x) signif(x, 4)),
                            check.names = FALSE)
other_like <- cbind(
  data.frame(Component = gsub("_", " ", rownames(tot_likes)[.keep]),
             check.names = FALSE),
  other_like)
rownames(other_like) <- NULL

flextable::flextable(other_like) |>
  # A dash marks a component the model does not have (see the NA note above);
  # it is not a fitted value of zero.
  flextable::colformat_double(na_str = "\u2013") |>
  # fontsize BEFORE autofit: autofit() measures the text at the CURRENT size, so
  # shrinking the font afterwards leaves the old, wider column widths in place.
  # set_table_properties(width=) does NOT constrain width in flextable 0.10.0 --
  # measured, it left these tables 13-22 in wide (2026-08-29).
  flextable::fontsize(size = 7, part = "all") |>
  flextable::autofit() |>
  flextable::set_caption(
    caption = paste("Remaining likelihood components (negative log-likelihood, dimensionless), one row",
      "per component and one column per model. These are the penalties, priors and data components",
      "that are not catch, index or size composition. Model 25.3 was fitted under GMACS 2.20.22, which",
      "reports the growth-increment likelihood in the Tagging row; 2.20.34 reports it under Growth.",
      "The two are the same quantity, so Model 25.3 does not have a tagging likelihood the others",
      "lack. The fall to about 4881 from Model 26.1a onward is the growth transcription fix."),
    autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "like-other-tot")
  )

```{r max-grad, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F}

## Turn a GMACS parameter name into something a reader can act on.
## "T_pars_est[3]" says nothing; the descriptive name GMACS carries for the same
## parameter is "Log(Rbar)". Expand the leading token and drop the underscores.
.pretty_par <- function(x) {
  if (is.na(x)) return(NA_character_)
  x <- sub("^Log\\(Rbar\\)$",     "log mean recruitment", x)
  x <- sub("^Log\\(R0\\)$",       "log unfished recruitment", x)
  x <- sub("^Log\\(Rinitial\\)$", "log initial recruitment", x)
  x <- sub("^Log\\((.*)\\)$",     "log \\1", x)
  x <- sub("^M_base_",  "base natural mortality, ", x)
  x <- sub("^M_",       "natural mortality, ", x)
  x <- sub("^Sel_",     "selectivity, ", x)
  x <- sub("^Initial_logN_for_sex_", "initial numbers at size, ", x)
  x <- sub("^Rec_",     "recruitment, ", x)
  x <- gsub("_", " ", x)
  x <- sub("block group 1 block ", "block ", x)
  x
}

extract_max_gradient <- function(path) {
  grad_file <- file.path(path, "gradient.dat")
  if (!file.exists(grad_file)) {
    return(data.frame(NPar = NA_integer_, Parameter = NA_character_,
                      Description = NA_character_, MaxAbsGradient = NA_real_))
  }
  grad <- read.table(grad_file, header = TRUE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  idx <- which.max(abs(grad$Gradient))

  ## GMACS's own descriptive name for the same parameter. The "--Estimated
  ## parameters" block of Gmacsall.out lists every parameter with a trailing
  ## index that counts only the ESTIMATED ones, and that index is the row number
  ## in gradient.dat -- verified 2026-08-29: 412 estimated parameters against 412
  ## gradient rows, with M_pars_est[15] resolving to
  ## M_female_immature_block_group_1_block_2, the parameter the convergence
  ## section discusses.
  desc <- NA_character_
  out_file <- file.path(path, "Gmacsall.out")
  if (file.exists(out_file)) {
    tmp <- readLines(out_file, warn = FALSE)
    st  <- grep("^--Estimated parameters: dataframe", tmp)[1]
    if (!is.na(st)) {
      for (ln in tmp[(st + 2):length(tmp)]) {
        if (!nzchar(trimws(ln)) || startsWith(ln, ">")) break
        f <- strsplit(trimws(ln), " +")[[1]]
        if (length(f) >= 11 && suppressWarnings(!is.na(as.integer(tail(f, 1)))) &&
            as.integer(tail(f, 1)) == idx) { desc <- sub(":$", "", f[2]); break }
      }
    }
  }

  data.frame(
    NPar           = nrow(grad),
    Parameter      = grad$ParName[idx],
    Description    = .pretty_par(desc),
    MaxAbsGradient = abs(grad$Gradient[idx])
  )
}

# models_present, not model_defs: extract_max_gradient() returns an all-NA row
# for a folder that does not exist, which would render as a blank row here.
gradlist <- list()
for(i in seq_along(models_present)){

  out <- extract_max_gradient(models_present[i])
 gradlist[[i]] <- data.frame(
    Model          = to_short(names(models_present)[i]),
    NPar           = out$NPar,
    Parameter      = out$Parameter,
    Description    = out$Description,
    MaxAbsGradient = round(out$MaxAbsGradient, 5)
  )
}
max_grad_df <- do.call("rbind", gradlist)
# Rows in model-number order. gradlist follows models_present, i.e. folder order,
# which since the 26.x renumbering puts 26.2 ahead of 26.1c and disagreed with
# every other table in the document (2026-08-29).
max_grad_df <- max_grad_df[order(max_grad_df$Model), ]

colnames(max_grad_df) <- c("Model", "N parameters", "Parameter", "What it is", "Max |gradient|")

flextable::flextable(max_grad_df) |>
  flextable::fontsize(size = 8, part = "all") |>
  flextable::autofit() |>
  ## Rescale to the 6.5 in portrait line; autofit alone sized this table
  ## wider than the page and clipped the right-hand columns (2026-09-08).
  flextable::fit_to_width(max_width = 6.4) |>
  flextable::set_caption(
    caption = "Maximum absolute gradient (dimensionless) for each model, and the parameter with the largest gradient. The Parameter column gives GMACS's internal name and \"What it is\" the quantity that name refers to: the T_pars (theta) block holds the recruitment scale and the initial numbers at size, M_pars natural mortality, S_pars selectivity and G_pars growth. A gradient of zero is the result of the Newton polishing described in the text. Model 25.3 could not be polished and is reported as originally fitted.",
    autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "max-grad")
  )
